title: Prosecutors gather volumes of evidence against Gold Coast developer
text:
Commonwealth prosecutors have gathered more than 90 witness statements and thousands of exhibits of evidence in their case against Gold Coast property developer David McWilliams.

Mr McWilliams was charged in June with 13 criminal offences related to an allegedly fraudulent $10 million NDIS property scheme.

The charges were laid after a two-year investigation by the Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC) into the activities of Mr McWilliams and his wife and business partner, Laura Fullarton.

ASIC alleges Mr McWilliams, as company director of ALAMMC Developments, dishonestly used investor funds earmarked for developing specialist disability accommodation projects in Queensland and Western Australia.

Investigators allege he spent more than $10 million on cryptocurrency, overseas investments, commercial and residential property and on a luxury sports car.

'Complications' with legal team

During a brief appearance in Southport Magistrates Court today, federal prosecutor Alice Tanzer-Wilde said 85 witness statements and more than 3,000 exhibits had been finalised and provided in a brief of evidence to Mr McWilliams's lawyers.

"There are still six witness statements outstanding, but we expect to be able to provide those by the 11th of September," Ms Tanzer-Wilde said.

Representing Mr McWilliams, Jack O'Callaghan told the court he was unsure if his firm would be retained at the next hearing date.

He said there were some "complications" with Mr McWilliams's ability to pay his legal fees.

"There are court-appointed receivers to Mr McWilliams's assets, so the release of funds for his representation is currently being resolved," Mr O'Callaghan said.

Mr McWilliams's assets were frozen in November 2024 by order of the Federal Court.

ASIC applied for Mr McWilliams to be held in contempt of those freezing orders in November 2025, after it alleged he and his wife spent hundreds of thousands of dollars on gambling and overseas trips.

An affidavit alleging further breaches of the freezing orders was then filed by ASIC in February.

In June, prior to being charged with any criminal offences, Mr McWilliams faced a four-day contempt hearing at the Federal Court in Brisbane, after which Justice O'Sullivan reserved his decision to a later date.

Mr McWilliams's ALAMMC group of companies wound up operations in October 2025 by order of the Federal Court.

Receivers appointed to the companies found Mr McWilliams had raised more than $90 million intended for disability housing projects, but that construction on most projects was either minimal or stopped entirely.

ASIC alleges ALAMMC Developments had started construction on only one of the six specialist accommodation projects linked to the charges.

Mr McWilliams's criminal charges return to Southport Magistrates Court in September.

title: Australian who died hiking US trail remembered as 'adventurous spirit'
text:
A Melbourne man who is believed to have fallen to his death while hiking a remote trail in the United States is being remembered for his love for adventure.

Will Standish, 28, had embarked on a hike through the Continental Divide Trail, which spans almost 5,000 kilometres between Mexico and Canada.

He was reported missing by his family after he failed to check in, with his body later discovered by a search and rescue crew last Wednesday, local time.

Mr Standish and Katie Jackson have hiked together. (Supplied: Katie Jackson )

One friend, Katie Jackson, said Mr Standish "had a uniquely large heart".

She said he had a love for adventure, tiny foster puppies, music, snowboarding, as well as for his family and friends.

"Will was a funny, adventurous spirit that brought laughter to every situation," she said.

"To be around him was to be infused with his unbridled joy for every aspect of life.

"[I am] incredibly grateful to have known Will so well and experienced how his life touched and changed mine."

Reported missing after failing to check-in

American authorities said Mr Standish had started his hike in Canada and was regularly updating his family in Australia via a satellite device.

He had updated his family on July 19, and provided them with details of his planned route.

The last update they received from Mr Standish, according to officials from Yellowstone and Grand Teton national parks, was four days later.

"The family received a Garmin check-in without coordinates or a message, as well as a video via Facebook Messenger that they believe placed him in the Tetons," officials said.

On July 27, his family contacted park officials raising concerns.

The Continental Divide National Scenic Trail spans almost 5,000 kilometres. (Supplied: Continental Divide Trail Coalition )

Two days later, on July 29, Teton County Search and Rescue located Mr Standish's body near an area known as the Wigwams on the west slop of the Tetons.

A helicopter had been sent to his last presumed point.

"From the air, the team spotted a bright orange backpack and soon found the subject below the ridge south of North Wigwam Peak," Teton County Search and Rescue said in a statement posted online.

"Evidence suggests that he may have fallen from a steep, high altitude ridgeline that separates Grand Teton National Park and the Jedediah Smith Wilderness."

Mr Standish has been described by fellow hikers as "competent, prepared and experienced".

He was an avid backpacker and climber, according to those who knew him.

Raising funds to bring Mr Standish home

The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade said it was providing consular assistance to Mr Standish's family.

"We send our deepest condolences to the family at this difficult time," a spokesperson said.

"Owing to our privacy obligations we are unable to provide further comment."

Ms Jackson said Mr Standish's family now faced "the immense challenge and financial burden of bringing him back to Australia".

"His sudden passing has left his family to navigate a painful loss that no family is ever truly prepared for," she said.

Ms Jackson has set up a crowdfunding page on behalf of Mr Standish's family, which is aiming to raise $US50,000 ($71,000) to assist the family with costs.

title: Big tech to pay more if no deal reached with Australian media
text:
Big tech companies that fail to strike commercial deals with Australian media organisations will face a 2.5 per cent levy on their digital advertising revenue under the federal government's proposed amendments to media bargaining laws, with legislation expected to be introduced to parliament within weeks.

However, the companies have secured a key concession, successfully arguing the levy should apply only to their digital advertising revenue.

That means while the penalty rate for failing to reach agreements with news organisations is higher than originally implemented, the amount companies would ultimately pay would be calculated on a much smaller portion of their overall revenue.

Big tech hits back at Labor's news payment plan US tech giant Meta has condemned Labor's plan to tax large digital platforms that fail to pay for using Australian journalism as "government-mandated transfer of wealth".

In the existing incentive structure, big digital search companies like Google would have paid a fee of 2.25 per cent of their revenue if they did not pay at least four local news companies under commercial agreements.

But they could avoid paying the fee if they entered into tax-deductible agreements worth about 1.5 per cent of their revenue.

The government has now changed the fee to 2.5 per cent of advertising revenue if companies do not come to agreements with at least six local news services.

AI companies will continue to be excluded from the scheme.

Assistant Treasurer Daniel Mulino said big tech companies should provide compensation to the organisations that provide them content through news.

"That will mean that we have a news production ecosystem that is more sustainable going forward," he said.

"This reflects the fact that what we are really trying to target here is the part of the business that uses the news."

Will big tech pay up?

Past attempts by the government to require big tech companies to pay for news have prompted threats to pull platforms from Australian users altogether.

Meta, which owns Facebook and Instagram, previously refused to renew deals with news organisations initially made under the News Media Bargaining Code, first introduced in 2021.

Meta instead effectively sidestepped the code by removing and de-prioritising news rather than being forced to pay for the content.

To address this loophole, the incentive scheme applies to major platforms regardless of whether they hosted news.

Mr Mulino said the scheme was designed to ensure that companies would end up paying more if they refused to strike deals, regardless of whether they hosted news on their platforms.

He also said he was "confident" companies would not choose to walk away altogether.

"Australia is one of the largest economies in the world, it's very profitable for them, and we are hearing no indications that would be their reaction," he said.

The amendments also mean the definition of journalists will be extended, broadening to include essential production roles and freelancers.

Start-ups have also gotten a nod, with 5 per cent of any fund raised through the News Bargaining Incentive to be funnelled into a grants program for small publishers and new starters.

The government has also increased the offset for deals with small publishers from 170 per cent to 200 per cent.

Anika Wells says the amendments will help regional news publishers remain sustainable. (ABC News: Joel Wilson)

Communications Minister Anika Wells said journalism was the "lifeblood" of a robust democracy.

She said the doubling of the distribution of scheme loading was critical to supporting regional publishers.

"This acknowledges both the challenges smaller outlets face, but also the incredible contribution they make to the communities they serve," she said.

title: Company wants to turn straw into fuel to ease reliance on Middle East
text:
Motorists will today go back to paying full price at the bowser after the four-month excise relief period runs out.

Despite repeated attempts at ceasefire agreements, the US-Iran conflict is still causing significant global oil price fluctuations, leaving Australia vulnerable and its drivers out of pocket.

One West Australian business says it is ready to pull Australia's fuel reliance away from the Middle East, and onto a new and environmentally friendly homegrown product.

Glas Energy is planning a $400 million commercial-scale renewable diesel refinery based in Narrogin, 180 kilometres south-east of Perth.

The site of the proposed renewable diesel processing plant, south of Narrogin. (ABC Great Southern: Mark Bennett)

Glas Energy's Nathan Carbone said while the product was organically sourced, it was equally efficient.

"[We are] looking to turn roughly 70,000 tonnes of straw and straw residuals into about 20 million litres of low-carbon liquid fuels," he said.

Nathan Carbone says the fuel product can operate independently of regular diesel. (ABC Great Southern: Mark Bennett)

"This is not the biodiesel of the 1990s. It burns clean. It is 100 per cent drop-in fuel.

"You can blend it with existing diesel at any rate."

While the product is not yet ready to hit the market, developers have asked the state and federal government for support.

Making the switch

While the plan looks environmentally sound, business owners do not want to be left short-changed.

WA trucking company KTrans operates a fleet of 150 heavy haulage trucks across the state, with the estimated fuel usage up to 1 million litres a month.

Executive general manager Daniel Burrows said renewable fuel was the next big thing for the company, but the numbers needed to line up.

Daniel Burrows says renewable fuel options need to match fossil fuel prices. (ABC Great Southern: Mark Bennett)

"All of our trucks come with renewable diesel in their tanks when we first purchase them," he said.

"We can swap tomorrow. We could replace our conventional diesel with renewable and wouldn't have to touch anything.

" [But] it's got to be commercially viable. It's got to be comparable to what we're paying now for diesel fuel. "

To do this, developers and interested parties have applied for the Clean Energy Future Fund, along with rallying state government representatives.

30 years of Esperance biofuels Esperance was once seen as a key location for a biofuel industry. Today some are trying to rebuild that dream.

"It does finance up to 50 per cent and we will contribute the other 50, so it's by no means a handout," Mr Carbone said.

"We're quite confident that we'll be seen in a positive light and we'll get a successful outcome out of that."

Keeping local

Beyond the environmental benefits, the initiative could bring tangible economic benefits to the regions.

Shire of Narrogin President Leigh Ballard said the project would benefit the local economy.

"One of the biggest things about this project is its circular economy," he said.

Leigh Ballard says the project will bring plenty of benefits for the region. (ABC Great Southern: Mark Bennett)

"It's going to be taking bioproducts from a farm, turning it into a fuel product and other farming products as well, which can then go back into the farming system."

Mr Carbone said the project would need to stay in the regions.

"We need to be near the feedstock purely because the amount of feedstock you need is significantly more than the fuel," he said.

"It doesn't really make much sense to source something, ship it hundreds of kilometres and then turn it into a low carbon fuel."

The developer is already looking at other locations across the state, with the Narrogin site acting as the central refinery.

Mr Ballard said producing these vital energy commodities would ensure Australia was not left as a victim of foreign conflicts.

Oil tankers stuck in the Strait of Hormuz are driving global fuel prices up. (Reuters)

"It's hugely important at the moment around our current fuel crisis, but also the future of our fuel supply in the country, and not being held over a barrel," he said.

"Being able to produce it locally, to supply it locally, is going to be a huge benefit for our state and our nation."

title: Tasmania's greyhound racing ban closer, some trainers keen on exit scheme
text:
Tasmania's new racing minister is said to be working "diligently" to get a ban on greyhound racing through parliament, as some racing participants express interest in the compensation scheme to leave the industry by the end of the year.

In April, the government deferred debate on legislation to ban greyhound racing when it appeared to be headed for defeat in the Legislative Council.

The government has said the bill will only go back to the upper house when it has the numbers to pass.

"We do need to end greyhound racing in Tasmania and we will," Premier Jeremy Rockliff said yesterday.

The three government MLCs, the Greens' Cassy O'Connor and independent Meg Webb have all confirmed they would support the bill.

Since April, independent Clare Glade-Wright has been elected to the upper house, and has confirmed she would also vote in support of the greyhound racing ban.

That gives the bill six of the eight votes it needs to pass.

With Clare Glade-Wright elected to the Legislative Council in May, the government now has seven of the eight votes it needs to pass the greyhound racing ban. (ABC News: Sophie Jaggers)

Independents Tania Rattray and Casey Hiscutt were planning to vote against the bill when it was before the Legislative Council in April, while fellow independent Bec Thomas spoke unfavourably about it.

With Labor opposed to the ban, the government would need the vote of at least two of the other independents — Ruth Forrest, Mike Gaffney or Rosemary Armitage.

A parliamentary committee, which had previously recommended the bill be passed with amendments, is doing further work following a request from Mr Rockliff.

That work includes examining:

Other jurisdictions' work to phase out greyhound racing.

The financial, economic and animal welfare impacts of the proposed phase out in Tasmania.

The future of the Tasmanian racing deed.

While the committee recommended the ban be supported, two members, Labor's Dean Winter and Ms Rattray, both signed dissenting statements.

It is expected the committee's work will be finished by October.

The greyhound racing sector nationally has been campaigning in support of the Tasmanian industry. (Supplied)

On Saturday, government minister Jo Palmer said Racing Minister Roger Jaensch — who was appointed to the role in June — had been "quite diligent in ensuring that he's communicating with those in the Legislative Council who still have questions about this piece of legislation".

"That work is ongoing," Ms Palmer said.

Roger Jaensch was appointed racing minister in June, and his colleague Jo Palmer says he's working "diligently" to address questions MLCs have about the ban. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

Racing participants express interest in leaving industry

While the legislation remains stalled, the government is pushing ahead with its proposed voluntary exit scheme, which will offer financial assistance and support to anyone who leaves the racing industry by the end of this year.

Tasmanian Racing Integrity Commissioner Sean Carroll said his office had so far received 13 submissions from participants asking for further information or expressing interest in the scheme.

"My office continues to consult directly with participants and stakeholders to understand individual circumstances and inform the development of the scheme," Mr Carroll said in a statement.

The greyhound races authorities don't want you to see If you watched greyhound race videos on Tasracing's website, you would likely never know that dozens of dogs were injured or killed during events last year.

According to information received by the Tasmanian Greens last month in response to questions asked during budget estimates hearings, there were 765 dogs in the state's greyhound racing industry.

The figures also showed there were 125 registered trainers in Tasmania, but a quarter of those do not have a dog registered to them, and 40 per cent of the greyhounds were registered to just 10 trainers.

A greyhound racing ban came into effect in New Zealand on Saturday, with chartered flights bringing up to 150 dogs from New Zealand to Australia where they will be able to keep racing.

Jeremy Rockliff says legislation to ban greyhound racing in Tasmania will allow for an "orderly transition". (ABC News: Kelsey Reid)

The Tasmanian government said it did not expect any New Zealand dogs to come to Tasmania given the impending ban.

Even without the legislation, Mr Rockliff has indicated the government would still end the industry by stopping its funding when the current deed expires in 2029.

But he said the legislation would provide for an "orderly transition to support animal welfare, support the dogs and support the industry".

Questions over cost

Labor's racing spokesperson, Dean Winter, on Saturday reaffirmed his party's opposition to banning greyhound racing.

Mr Winter also said it was unclear how much the phasing out of greyhound racing would cost.

"What is the compensation going to be, how much is it going to cost Tasmania's budget that is already in all sorts of trouble," he said.

Anti-greyhound racing campaigners protested outside Labor's state conference in April. (ABC News: Mitch Woolnough)

The government has budgeted $4.6 million for "greyhound racing transition" over the next four years, but Labor has concerns the cost of rehoming greyhounds will cost far more than that.

"To my knowledge the only modelling that's been done is for 1,000 greyhounds and if you were to rehome them under the model that New Zealand's taken, it would cost Tasmanian taxpayers around $40 million," Mr Winter said.

Mr Rockliff said "the figures put forward by the national greyhound industry and indeed Dean Winter are fanciful".

"We will work with the industry; we have a budget that has been outlined in terms of compensation and transition."

Ms O'Connor, who is the Tasmanian Greens' animal rights spokesperson, also disputed the $40 million figure.

"Of course, there'll be up-front costs from ending greyhound racing and rehoming the hundreds of dogs it uses up, but there will no doubt be significant savings in ending the public subsidies after the phase-out," she said today in a statement.

" What we do know is that keeping greyhound racing on life support will cost Tasmanian taxpayers more than phasing it out. "

Ms O'Connor also called on Labor leader Josh Willie to allow the Labor upper house members a conscience vote on this issue when it returns to parliament.

title: Geopolitical tensions at forefront of mining forum in WA outback city
text:
As its name would suggest, the Diggers and Dealers Mining Forum brings together opposing sides of Australia's resources sector, those at the coalface carrying a shovel and financial backers with a briefcase.

As industry heavyweights descend on Kalgoorlie-Boulder for the 35th edition of the famous conference, bars and boardrooms in the historic gold mining city will be filled for three days as many a deal gets done.

But one company that will not be spotted on the sidelines is the taxpayer-backed Iluka Resources, which is building a $1.8 billion rare earths refinery in WA's Midwest.

Dan McGrath says about 90 per cent of the world's rare earths are supplied by China. (ABC Perth: Glyn Jones)

As Iluka's head of rare earths, Dan McGrath, explained, the company shakes hands on deals in private, out of necessity.

"We've got a lot of discussions ongoing with a lot of parties, but all of those discussions are confidential because right now those supply chains rely on rare earths from China," he said.

"Discussions may result in the risk of China cutting off the supply between now and when our rare earths are available next year, so we keep those discussions very confidential."

First deal of many

In June, the Perth-headquartered Iluka signed its first offtake deal with an unnamed global car maker to supply magnet rare earth oxides from 2028.

The $US155 million ($220 million) deal is set to underpin the first four years of operations at Iluka's Eneabba refinery, which is about 60 per cent built near the small farming community about 280 kilometres north of Perth.

Once commissioned, the plant will churn out products like neodymium, praseodymium, terbium and dysprosium, which are critical in the manufacture of high-tech magnets found in electric vehicles, wind turbines and weaponry.

The $1.8 billion Eneabba rare earths refinery is on track for commissioning next year. (Supplied: Iluka Resources)

Critical mineral supply chains, but particularly rare earths, have become a focal point for many Western governments in recent years.

In the case of the Eneabba refinery, the project is backed by a $1.65 billion loan from the federal government's Critical Minerals Facility.

Mr McGrath said Australia's relationship with the United States was a critical component moving forward.

Anthony Albanese and Donald Trump signed an $8.5 billion rare earth minerals agreement in 2025. (Getty Images: Anna Moneymaker)

"The world needs more rare earths and those manufacturing supply chains are currently captive to the whim of the Chinese government, which has had a tendency over the years to weaponise the rare earths supply chain," he said.

"Australia and other like-minded and economically liberal nations realise that their own domestic, sovereign manufacturing capacity needs a source of rare earths that's outside of China.

"We're not just talking to the US, we're talking to European, Japanese and other countries all over the globe."

Trade being 'weaponised'

The growing geopolitical tensions were reflected in July when the federal government signed an agreement to supply more uranium to India.

India's High Commissioner to Australia, Canberra-based Nagesh Singh, said ongoing cooperation among nations would be vital in lifting living standards in his country.

Nagesh Singh wants more collaboration between like-minded countries on critical minerals. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

During a brief stopover in Kalgoorlie-Boulder on Thursday, Mr Singh toured the $800 million Kalgoorlie refinery owned by the Gina Rinehart-backed Lynas Rare Earths.

"I am not naming any countries but trade, resources are being weaponised … so like-minded countries who share common geopolitical objectives are coming together the world over," he said.

"You'll see more and more cooperation happening. It's going to be a very critical area for future growth, not just for India and Australia, but the rest of the world.

"These specific minerals should be democratised, everyone should have access without the threat of denial."

title: Ex-NRL player reveals betting companies offered to arrange illegal drugs
text:
A former professional rugby league player says gambling company employees offered to secure him illicit drugs to "strengthen" their relationship when he was in the grips of a financially crippling wagering addiction.

Luke Bateman, 31, who had losses of "tens of thousands of dollars a month" at the peak of his problem gambling, will give evidence about his personal experience at a Senate inquiry into the federal government's legislation to restrict gambling ads in Canberra on Monday.

Luke Bateman reveals depths of gambling habit Luke Bateman was 19 and living out his NRL dream, but a gambling addiction saw him retire from sport $250,000 in debt.

The two-day inquiry is due to hear from medical experts and welfare charities urging Labor to strengthen its proposal, while the gambling industry has argued against tougher measures.

Bateman, who played in the NRL for the Canberra Raiders and is now a social media influencer with a two-book deal to author his own fantasy series, last month told Australian Story how he survived his gambling addiction and was now advocating for an end to so-called gambling inducements.

Members of the crossbench, opposition and some backbench government MPs are also backing this push, while last month delegates at Labor's national conference voted to include a commitment to tackle inducements in the party's policy platform.

The government's legislation proposes restrictions on TV gambling ads between 6am and 8:30pm and on radio during school pick-up and drop-off times, as well as an opt-out system for online ads.

'Relentless' gambling inducements take their toll

Bateman previously held multiple online wagering accounts across several companies and said as a high-spending punter he was assigned account managers as a personalised point of contact.

He said these managers would seek to build a rapport with him, offering gambling inducements, like bonus bets, and invitations to exclusive events with travel, hotels, food and alcohol all paid for.

Luke Bateman says the promotion of inducements was "relentless". (Australian Story: Tom Hancock)

"They enter into this knowing that the reason that they are creating a friendship with you is to encourage you to bet with them and to continue to lose lots and lots of money," he said.

"They are not doing it out of any duty of care."

Bateman described the promotion of inducements as "relentless".

"I was a racing punter. Obviously, Saturdays are your main race days, so every Friday I would receive a message of, 'Hello, this is your exclusive offer for tomorrow,'" he said.

"That would happen every single week."

Drugs offered in bid to build personal relationships

Bateman has also alleged there were "multiple times" when, after accepting an invitation to an interstate event, he would be contacted by his gambling account manager offering to arrange access to illicit drugs.

"The week of the event, they'd sort of send you a message and be like, 'Hey mate, you know, do you want any … drugs on the weekend?'" he said.

" If you're going to Melbourne, they're like, 'Hey mate … if you need a couple of bags, let us know and we'll have it organised for you and we'll get it to you.' "

Bateman said these offers were not made in any "official" capacity on behalf of the wagering companies, but he believed it was a "tactic" to "strengthen friendships and bonds" with his account manager.

"That obviously … came with the expectation that then I would continue to gamble with their company specifically, and nobody else," he said.

"Creating a sense of trust, creating a sense of friendship, absolutely came with the underlying desire to make sure that you lost all of your money with them.

Luke Bateman played for the Canberra Raiders from 2015 to 2020. (Getty Images: Mark Nolan)

Bateman said illicit drugs were a part of the "sporting, partying male culture in general" that was "part and parcel" with the "racing, sporting drinking sort of scene".

"That was happening in all areas of life," he said.

"I was also like a very happy and willing participant of this. No-one was forcing me to do this.

" But I was also 21, very young, very vulnerable and these men [working for the gambling companies] were older, in positions of power … I would say really exploiting that vulnerability and youthful naivety. "

Bateman tells inquiry he took drugs with gambling CEO

Bateman on Monday told the Senate hearing he was invited to an exclusive event hosted at a rental property on the Gold Coast where he took illicit drugs with senior members of the gambling company.

"The entire sort of C-suite of the company was there, all management team, administration, and they were all sort of in the back room doing drugs together, and I was in this room doing drugs with all of them," he said.

"This is like the CEO, the founders, the VIP managers, and you know at that stage I would have been a 23-year-old."

A visibly shocked ACT independent Senator David Pocock asked Bateman to confirm that not only account managers working on commission, but senior levels of the gambling companies were aware of the behaviour.

Bateman responded: "Not only did they know, they were participating in it."

Mark Kempster, who is a "lived experience advocate" with the Alliance for Gambling Reform, then told the hearing he knew "dozens of examples" like the one described by Bateman.

"That is a regular thing that happens across nearly all of the major VIP programs that I've seen," he said.

In an unrelated case, Alliance for Gambling Reform chief advocate Reverend Tim Costello told the inquiry TAB and Sportsbet had funded travel, escorts and drugs for a high-spending gambler who was now in Silverwater prison on charges related to the theft of about $12.3 million.

Rev Costello said the man was preparing to plead guilty to stealing the money from his company over a 17-month period to fund a serious gambling addiction.

He said during this time Star Casino frequently gave the man free accommodation.

"He was the TAB's biggest customer in that time. They were giving him $50,000 bonus bets," he added.

"He was also Sportsbet's biggest customer.

"They were flying him to grand finals. They were offering him escorts, drugs, whatever he wanted. He was doing turnover of more than $20 million a month."

Mr Costello did not name the man, but said he would provide character evidence for him in court.

Inducements make it hard to 'break away'

Bateman said when he was losing tens of thousands of dollars, his account managers did not offer help, seek to verify what his earnings were or indicate he should seek support.

Instead, he said there were times after a "big loss" he would be contacted with a bonus bet offer where the company would tip in an additional amount of funds to gamble with.

Gambling advertising crackdown The Albanese government will target social media influencers and individuals who promote gambling on social media as part of its proposed laws.

"When someone reaches out to you and offers you … this really attractive deal to do it again, it's so motivating to re-enter gambling," he said.

Bateman said the inducements were also "incredibly triggering" when he was trying to "break away" from the patterns, people and places linked to his addiction.

Despite his experience, Bateman said he had a lot of "grace" for the account managers who were just doing their job.

"I'm not going to sit here and say that these people are completely evil, but the industry creates the opportunity for this to happen," he said.

" These people are really just existing inside of the vacuum created by lack of regulation. "

Bateman said he would like to see the government remove promotions and inducements sent by text, email or phone call, whether as a mass-marketing campaign or through personalised account managers.

"Removing those direct contacts and those direct promotions and inducements would be incredibly helpful," he said.

"It's not [about] trying to stop anyone from having a bet.

"What we're trying to stop is the relentless targeting of vulnerable individuals."

Under Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, Labor is pushing forward with its gambling reform. (ABC News: Adam Kennedy)

Labor stands by 'strongest-ever' reforms

A spokesperson for the federal government said Labor was focused on implementing its proposal, described as the "strongest-ever" reforms to tackle gambling harms.

"Among these measures is a strengthening of BetStop, the national register that allows people who don't want to place a bet or get inducements to opt out," they said.

"There are also existing restrictions on gambling companies for inducements, including that direct marketing may only be sent to customers who have provided their consent to receive them."

This Liberal took his teacher to gambling anonymous When Liberal backbencher Simon Kennedy was a teenager, one of his high school teachers asked to borrow money for his gambling addiction. He says he ended up accompanying the teacher to Gamblers Anonymous meetings.

But Liberal MP Simon Kennedy said the gambling industry had shown self-regulation did not work despite the government leaving "predatory gambling inducements out of its reforms".

"Labor's own national conference has recognised the problem," he said.

"Now the prime minister needs to show the same leadership."

In submissions to the Senate inquiry, St Vincent de Paul Society CEO Toby O'Connor also said "stronger action" was needed, while the Royal Australasian College of Physicians called for an end to online gambling advertising.

Meanwhile, peak industry body Responsible Wagering Australia (RWA) has said Labor's proposal will "materially reduce funding for broadcasting, sport and racing" and argued the measures went "further than required" to meet the government's objectives.

"This will reduce funding flowing to sport, local clubs, community programs and racing," the RWA submission said.

RWA said illegal offshore gambling was a growing "threat" and argued reforms should be "carefully calibrated" to avoid pushing consumers toward these markets that were "beyond the reach of the very protections Australia has established to keep them safe".

title: Quick hits: Delta stuns with Aussie classic, 76yo claims history-making gold
text:
Delta Goodrem belts out an Aussie classic, a 76-year-old makes Commonwealth Games history and a cycling star is proud to have not thrown up on the podium.

Here are the quick hits from day nine of the Commonwealth Games.

1. Delta makes it a hat-trick with Aussie classic

Delta Goodrem produced a breathtaking performance in the closing ceremony. (Getty Images: Mattia Ozbot)

It was a closing ceremony featuring some serious Australian star power, with Delta Goodrem headlining proceedings.

It was the third time, after Melbourne 2006 and Gold Coast 2018, that Goodrem had performed at a Commonwealth Games, and the Australian icon was in fine form at the Hydro indoor arena in Glasgow.

Goodrem was revealed to the crowd in dramatic fashion, lit by a spotlight and sitting at a grand piano, belting out her classic Born To Try, before rising from her seat and welcoming the athletes into the venue with an inspired medley of her hits.

And the performance reached a real crescendo when she welcomed Scottish pop star Cammy Barnes to the stage for a rendition of the most classic of Aussie classics, John Farnham's You're the Voice.

Goosebumps in Glasgow.

2. 76-year-old creates Games history

Louise Hoskins made history on the final day of competition. (Getty Images: Adam Pretty)

Louise Hoskins, 76, made history on the final day of competition in Glasgow, becoming the oldest medal winner in Commonwealth Games history.

She, along with partner Serena Bonnell, won gold in the women's Para bowls, defeating New Zealand in a classic.

It was Bonnell who provided the winning moment for the Aussies, conjuring a sublime shot late in the second set to secure the win.

The oldest competitor in Glasgow, Hoskins was struggling to wrap her head around the enormity of the achievement.

"It is incredible. I'm still pinching myself," she said.

"I never thought I'd ever get [a gold medal] at my age. Get out there and have a go, and never give up."

Asked how she planned to celebrate, Hoskins noted Bonnell still owed her a few drinks.

What will it be then?

"Whatever Serena's going to give me," Hoskins laughed.

3. Cycling star proud not to spew on podium

Leigh Hoffman looked far from comfortable on the podium. (Getty Images: Rob Casey/SNS Group)

Australian Leigh Hoffman won four medals in a packed track cycling program, including a gold on the final day of competition.

He was the second-last rider in the men's 1,000m time trial, so had a truncated warm-down before climbing onto the podium to receive his gold medal.

And he looked far from comfortable on the top step.

"You don't feel human," he says.

"You're just so cooked, my legs are still burning right now, I think it's been a solid hour. There's no pain like it for sprint and endurance – 1 kilometre all-out sprint, 58 seconds of pure pain. I'm still feeling it.

"I made sure to eat about four hours out so my stomach was pretty empty. I'm proud I didn't spew."

This is the sprint and keirin specialist's first 1km time trial in six years, but he says he has no plans to keep riding them at world titles, although he may go again in Amdavad in four years' time.

4. Aussie chef de mission gets ink

Loading...

Australia's chef de mission Petria Thomas loves the Friendly Games — and understandably so.

She was a nine-time Commonwealth gold medallist during her decorated swimming career and has just overseen a Games in which Australia claimed 70 golds, 41 more than the next best nation, England.

On the final day of competition, Thomas was seen out in Glasgow getting herself a permanent testament to the event for which she has so much affection.

She said the Games have a special place in her heart, and now a special place on her body.

"I've thought about it for a long time and the Commonwealth Games has been such a big part of my life, as big a part as the Olympics. So I thought why not get the Commonwealth Sport mark as well, and I'll wear it very proudly," Thomas said.

"The Commonwealth Games has played such an important part of my life and I wanted to get something to remember that."

5. Scottish athletes win fashion stakes

Scottish athletes had some fun at the closing ceremony. (AP: Kin Cheung)

Scottish athletes were hard to miss at the closing ceremony.

The host nation's contingent wore traffic cones on their heads as they took part in the festivities inside The Hydro.

Loading Instagram content

It's common practice for Glaswegians to put traffic cones on the heads of statues around the city.

Arguably the most famous example is the Duke of Wellington statue outside the Gallery of Modern Art.

A statue in Boston could not escape the Glaswegian tradition during the FIFA World Cup. (Getty Images: Craig Williamson/SNS Group)

The ritual was celebrated at the recent FIFA World Cup, with Scottish fans decorating statues in Boston in their customary way.

You can never suggest Scots don't know how to poke fun at themselves.

ABC/AAP

title: Blues pay tribute to 'hero' Daley as he stands down as coach
text:
Laurie Daley has ended speculation about his future by stepping down as NSW State of Origin coach after a series victory over Queensland.

After much speculation about his future, Daley took the expected step and announced the move in a statement from the NSWRL.

"I've always considered it an absolute honour and privilege to be involved with the NSW Blues State of Origin team, whether that was as a player or a coach, and I've always been ready to answer the call for my state whenever they needed me," Daley said.

Daley slams 'hidden agendas' after NSW Origin win Laurie Daley has the last laugh over critics who hounded him ahead of the State of Origin decider at Lang Park.

"We faced plenty of challenges in the 2026 series and I'm proud of the way the players banded together to overcome them and save their best performance for Game Three in Brisbane to secure a memorable series win.

"I thank the fans for their passion and their support, and I can't think of a better way to move on with the Shield back where it belongs in NSW."

The NSWRL paid tribute to Daley for his time with the team.

"NSWRL owes a massive debt of gratitude to Laurie for the service he has given to his state as both a player and a coach," NSWRL chief executive David Trodden said.

"He is widely regarded as one of the greatest players to have ever pulled on a sky blue jumper, becoming the first NSW captain to lead his state to three consecutive series wins in 1992-94.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"He has also led NSW to arguably two of the greatest Origin series wins of all time as a coach, after ending Queensland's eight-year winning streak in 2014 and overcoming adversity to steer the Blues home in 2026.

"Those wins transcended football. They lifted and reinvigorated the whole state. He deserves to leave the NSW Origin arena as the hero that he is."

After sealing the State of Origin series win, Daley delivered a scathing rebuke to his critics, suggesting there were "hidden agendas" that attempted to undermine his NSW camp.

Daley, hammered publicly and privately over the Blues' form through the first two games of the series, had the last laugh as NSW secured a 30-12 victory at Lang Park.

title: Commonwealth Games don't need to mean anything to you to mean the world
text:
You see a lot of Olympic rings tattoos on athletes.

They feature a lot in the pool and the track, as you'd expect, but you'll catch them on NRL and NRLW players too from time to time, thanks to the recent inclusion of rugby sevens.

Petria Thomas got them on her right ankle 30 years ago and, after Glasgow, she's had the 2026 Commonwealth Games logo inked on the other side.

"The Commonwealth Games has been such a big part of my life, as big a part as the Olympics, so I thought why not?" the eight-time Olympic medallist said.

"I'll wear it very proudly."

Loading...

Thomas, who won nine golds across three Commonwealth outings, said the 1994 Games were the springboard for her career, just as they will be for so many athletes in Glasgow.

"For many athletes, this is their first experience in a multi-sport environment and there's nothing that can compare to going into those sorts of environments," she said.

"So to have the opportunity to do it here in Glasgow has been incredible and for so many of our Australian athletes, the Commonwealth Games is their launching pad."

The 2026 Games will forever mark the coming out party for debutant athletes as varied as 14-year-old Mia Hogan, a girl who made the final of the women's 100m freestyle S13 on the first night of the swimming program, and 76-year-old Louise Hoskins, Australia's oldest gold medallist after para pairs bowls victory in the final hours of competition.

At 76, Games debutant Louise Hopkins is Australia's oldest gold medallist. (Getty Images: Adam Pretty)

For the rising athletics team, this was a combination of a coming of age and a coming out, with the middle-distance, long-distance and field stars reaffirming their brilliance, and the newly minted sprint stars shining at an international meet for the first time.

Even in the swimming team, with so many established stars who regularly speak about the Commonwealth Games as a stepping stone, there were people like Jenna Forrester and Sam Williamson and Meg Harris getting their moments in the sun.

At times it felt like an unfair fight.

Shayna Jack, Meg Harris and Mollie O'Callaghan made just one of the podium sweeps for the Australian team. (Gety Images: Ross MacDonald/SNS Group)

In the end, Australia led the overall medal tally by a cool 61 medals, winning more than twice as many golds as England and more than triple Canada's after topping the swimming, cycling and athletics.

It's true that some of the best sporting nations weren't here and of those that were, some of the superstars didn't turn up, but you can only beat the ones who do.

"We're just good at our sport. Everyone likes an underdog. We're the same in Australia," Thomas said.

"Australians really value Commonwealth Games, it's always been an important competition for us and our sports know how important it is for athlete development and career progression. We really have prioritised Commonwealth Games and that's really shown here."

And try telling Peter Bol that these Games don't matter as he cheered on Luke Boyes and Peyton Craig on their way to the 800m final.

It mattered to Peter Bol. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Try telling Paul Trainor not to worry as he processed being battered by Dimeji Shittu in their heavyweight semifinal.

It mattered to Paul Trainor. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Try telling Kiana Elliott to cheer up after her third clean and jerk left her fourth for a second straight Games.

It mattered to Kiana Elliott. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Try telling Georgia Baker her spectacular Games weren't worth anything as she burst into tears when receiving the news she was the closing ceremony flag-bearer.

It mattered to Georgia Baker. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

These Games can mean government waste to Victorians, they can mean occasional traffic inconveniences to Glaswegians, they can mean late nights or early mornings on a blog or stream for many of you.

But they can also mean a new beginning, for athletes young and old, and for the Games as a whole.

Ironically, the event that Thomas credits for kickstarting her international career 32 years ago, was held in Victoria, albeit the one in Canada. This time around, the Australian version's withdrawal led to Glasgow picking up the baton.

Fans gather near Glasgow's Finnieston Crane between Games events. (Getty Images: Euan Cherry)

Limited and imperfect, it was a decision that saved a concept on life support.

"We're just grateful to be here," Thomas said, getting choked up.

"After what occurred, there was a time where we didn't know whether there would ever be another Commonwealth Games."

Commonwealth Sport has pledged to keep the Games alive.

It wants to engage with athletes to make them fit for purpose and sustainable, economically and environmentally.

Amdavad in India has pledged to deliver a full slate of events in 2030, with prospective hosts allegedly expressing interest in taking on 2034.

Who knows if that will come to fruition, but for 10 days of inclement weather and imperfect organisation, we saw a glimpse of Australia's future, and that's got to be worth something.

title: Hundreds gather at Harts Range for red dirt racing and rodeo
text:
In the desert sand beneath the towering ranges, more than 1,200 ringers, pastoralists and residents from across the Red Centre gathered on the weekend for the Harts Range Rodeo and Races.

The iconic outback event takes place on Mount Riddock cattle station near the remote community of Atitjere, about a 220-kilometre drive north-east from Alice Springs.

Now in their 79th year, the races have been bringing people together in this remote part of the country for decades.

Riders showcased their steeds to spectators before taking to the track. (ABC Rural: Charles Geary)

A chance to reconnect

For people living on remote Territory cattle stations, events like the past weekend's are rare opportunities to spend time with friends face-to-face.

The future of rodeo was in safe hands at Harts Range. (ABC Rural: Charles Geary)

This year, many stations in the region are celebrating their best season in recent memory due to significant rainfall.

But others are still recovering from damaging historic flooding from the start of the year.

Harts Range Races life member Jo Fogarty is from Lucy Creek Station, which is still working through repairs.

Jo Fogarty says it has been nice to see everyone after a particularly heavy wet season. (ABC Rural: Charles Geary)

"Especially this area with all the rain people have had, it's good just to get together and have a yarn," Ms Fogarty said.

"When you're [at] the beginning of the year when everyone's talking about the floods [and] now it's like, oh, let's just have a good time," she said.

"We're a pretty good community and everyone is very caring."

Will Weir and Alan Brown helped organise the bucking stock on the day. (ABC Rural: Charles Geary)

Good-natured competition

As well as lots of racing, the weekend hosts fashion on the field events, family activities and a Saturday night bush dance.

The rodeo events attract seasoned competitors as well as more recently arrived young ringers living and working in the region.

Anthony and Danyelle Haigh took out one of the Fashions on the Field events at the Central Australian race meet. (ABC Rural: Charles Geary)

Jacob Portelli is from Sydney, and is a first-year ringer at Huckitta Station, where his brother is the station manager.

He said local rodeos like these will keep him in the region a little longer.

"I want to give it a crack and try and win meself one of them [trophy belt] buckles," Mr Portelli said.

Bronco riders were assisted by pickup men from local cattle stations. (ABC Rural: Charles Geary)

"[It] might not be next year, but I think I'm stuck here until I get one of them."

In the horse racing, Jake Dallaglio took out the feature Stockman's Cup, having struggled in the earlier races in the afternoon.

Jake Dallaglio took out the feature Stockman’s Cup on Saturday afternoon. (ABC Rural: Charles Geary)

Finishing the race as the sun set over Harts Range, he said it was a good way to end the racing.

"First race didn't go so well, [I] came second last," Mr Dallaglio said.

"[So] to win, that's a pretty cool feeling."

title: Morocco blames social media, human traffickers for Spain migrant rush
text:
Morocco's Interior Ministry says the recent mass crossing of migrants into the Spanish ​enclaves ‌of Ceuta and Melilla was fuelled by misinformation on social media, ‌human trafficking ⁠networks and misinterpretation of ‌a Spanish court ruling.

About 40,000 people were involved ​in ‌the rush into Ceuta and ⁠1,135 were ‌stopped from entering ‌Melilla, the ministry said in ‌a statement.

Migrants gather around a torched vehicle as they wait for a chance to enter Ceuta on Friday. (Reuters: Stringer)

At least 11 people died while trying to cross the border, the ministry said. The figure was significantly smaller than that provided by the Spanish government, which on Sunday said it had recovered 72 bodies, up from the 67 it had previously reported.

Italy takes 'extraordinary' action after Ceuta migrant rush Tens of thousands of migrants crossed from Morocco into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta in chaotic scenes that left dozens dead.

However, Morocco's death toll may have been limited to those deaths occurring on the Moroccan side of the border, with the ministry adding that it was fact-checking reports of more deaths across the border.

The statement otherwise echoed comments from Spanish Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska, who over the weekend blamed people-smuggling networks for exploiting vulnerable migrants by spreading misleading interpretations of a recent Spanish Supreme Court ruling.

The ruling said migrants intercepted at sea could not be summarily returned in the absence of a physical barrier.

"Morocco isn't any threat to Ceuta or the rest of Spain. It's a fully reliable partner," he said, adding there had been no intelligence indicating a mass entry was imminent.

Loading...

While the vast majority of the migrants who entered Ceuta left within 48 hours, the mass crossing caused alarm across the European Union, prompting 22 of its member states to call for coordinated action to protect external borders and other measures.

Italy also suspended passport-free Schengen travel arrangements with Spain for a month, prompting criticism from Spain's centre-left prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, who had already confirmed those who entered Ceuta irregularly would not be able to travel onwards to mainland Spain.

"In the current international context, the EU cannot afford this kind of selfish, polarising and unlawful reaction," Mr Sánchez wrote in a letter to the EU Commission and European Council presidents.

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has criticised Italy for banning travel from Spain for a month. (Reuters: Fabian Bimmer)

On Saturday, Spanish police began installing a 500-metre floating barrier off its border with Morocco, blocking the Tarajal breakwater, one of the main points used by Moroccans trying to enter Ceuta.

The AUGC union for Spain's Civil Guard gendarmerie also said it was asking for reinforcements of at least 200 officers and warned that more work was needed to stop people swimming around the barrier.

Reuters/ABC

title: Vehicle with 1 million kilometres on the clock hits the market
text:
After clocking 1 million kilometres in his four-wheel-drive vehicle, a west Victorian stock agent has listed his prized possession for sale.

Nhill resident Gary Driscoll averaged more than 180km a day in his 2009 Toyota LandCruiser, driving to properties across the west of the state.

The vehicle goes up for sale on Monday morning, with an online auction to run for two weeks.

Mr Driscoll said he could not put a figure on the vehicle's value.

"I don't think anyone's got any particular value of what it's worth; it's what it's worth to [the buyer]," he said.

"Everyone's going to get a chance to have a go at it and practically whatever it makes it makes.

" I would have thought that it should make $30,000-plus, so the value will be in the eyes of the beholder. "

Gary Driscoll with his LandCruiser that is 300 metres shy of the 1 million kilometre mark. (Supplied: Gary Driscoll)

The digital odometer of the LandCruiser, which is currently parked in Nhill, reads 999,999km.

Mr Driscoll decided not to click it over the 1 million-kilometre mark.

"The old girl's now retired as far as I'm concerned and she's got about 300 metres to go to get to the million mark," he said.

" I'm going to allow the purchaser to have the privilege of driving that 300 metres. "

Mr Driscoll said he did not know what would happen to the odometer once it ticked over.

"I'm not sure that Toyota even know because I don't think there's been another 200 series that has done it.

"So whether it goes back to all zeros … Toyota have got the feeling that it might just stay on all the nines, but we won't know until someone gets in it and goes for a drive."

The Horsham Toyota dealership said the vehicle had been serviced almost 100 times and it was the most travelled car it had seen.

The dealership said it was the first vehicle it had seen that had hit the 1 million-kilometre mark, particularly with the original engine.

The manufacturer was unable to confirm the highest mileage Toyota vehicle in Australia, but said it was aware of several customers whose Toyota vehicles had passed the 1 million-kilometre mark.

The odometer shows 999,999 kilometres on Gary Driscoll's LandCruiser. (Supplied: Gary Driscoll)

Cruiser on 'rare road'

Automotive journalist Toby Hagon said it was "extremely rare" to find a car that had driven 1 million kilometres, let alone for that car to be put up for auction.

"Plenty of cars, once they're getting to 200,000 to 300,000km, that can be seen as a high-mileage car," he said.

"Obviously, a lot can go wrong with a car in that time and if you think about how much driving that is, it's a heck of a lot of time on the road.

"The only [cars] I've really ever seen that are over a million kilometres [on the main market websites] are where people have incorrectly put the wrong odometer in there.

" It's not something that comes up too often. I would think you'd see a car like this every few years at best. "

He said it was "really tricky" to put a value on the car, but said LandCruisers did hold their value extremely well.

"How old the car is and how far it's driven directly impacts what it's worth," Mr Driscoll said.

"The car itself ordinarily might be worth $30,000 to 35,000, somewhere around that, but that's for a car with maybe less than half those kilometres on it.

"I'm not sure there'd be a whole lot of people lining up for that because obviously the usefulness of the car and how much more you're going to get out of it will be diminished compared with a similar car with [fewer] kilometres on it.

"So, maybe it might get $20,000 to $30,000 if someone decides there is a bit of fun factor to it."

Mr Hagon said it was more likely for a 4WD or a ute to clock over 1 million kilometres, as they did long trips on country roads.

"Sitting on a country road is a lot more gentle on a car, on an engine, than zipping around town at lower speeds," he said.

"So, that's part of the reason you tend to get these higher kilometres, higher mileage out of cars like that."

title: Outback businesses blame Live Traffic NSW for customer downturn
text:
Living and working in the outback can be isolating, but for small businesses dependent on tourism, long-term damage to major roads can spell the end.

Lately, the problem has been further exacerbated by incorrect information on traffic websites that tell travellers if roads and highways are open, business owners say.

Mia Degoumois, who has owned the Packsaddle Roadhouse for the past 24 years, said a lack of tourists was causing "a massive downturn in business".

Located 175 kilometres north of Broken Hill, Ms Degoumois said the Live Traffic NSW website and app were confusing people.

"Information doesn't seem to catch up," she said.

" You get good local reports which are accurate, but sometimes it seems they don't flow on to Live Traffic and that's not a good thing, especially when everyone's being told that's the go-to to get your information. "

Mia Degoumois says the inaccuracies are discouraging potential customers. (ABC Broken Hill: Jonathon Poulson)

Her visitation figures are down by about an eighth this winter, usually the peak tourism season for the outback.

And with her sales from the past six months down by about $200,000, Ms Degoumois and other remotely located small businesses are partially attributing the revenue loss to incorrect information on Live Traffic NSW.

"I don't really know what the problem is. I can't see why it is a problem, like, why they can't fix it and make it easy," she said.

"A lot of times it feels like you're so far outback that no-one really cares unless they want to travel [here]."

Major roads finally reopen after heavy rainfall

Following months of record rainfall in remote parts of New South Wales, South Australia and Queensland, major roads in far west NSW, including the Silver City Highway between Broken Hill and Tibooburra, have only just fully reopened for the first time since March.

But Live Traffic NSW is taking a while to reflect these updates.

Additionally, due to the website and app only having two options — open or closed — roads and highways that are open to 4WD only are incorrectly listed as "closed".

The Silver City Highway, between Broken Hill and Tibooburra, earlier this year after heavy rain. (Supplied: Jessica Woods)

According to Transport for NSW, roads will only show as being open when they are accessible to all vehicles.

A Transport for NSW spokesperson said safety was its highest priority and that both sealed and unsealed roads throughout the far west had been damaged due to extensive rainfall, with several roads remaining closed.

They added that crews were continuing to actively inspect and repair the roads and the department was continually looking for ways to improve the disruption information provided to the public.

Outback business on the brink

In the 26 years Rebecca Young has owned the Milparinka Hotel, she said this season has been her worst year of trade.

She has blamed inaccurate road information.

Rebecca Young says the issues with Live Traffic NSW are affecting her business. (Supplied: Rebecca Young)

With her pub located located 125km north of Packsaddle, most of her revenue comes from travellers passing through the Silver City Highway, but this year, traffic has been down 80 to 90 per cent, and she is unsure if she will still be open in six months.

"It's going to be very tough getting through the summer months not having that income during the tourist season," Ms Young said.

" Hopefully I can come out on the other side of it, but I don't know. "

Kathy Brown says she receives hundreds of calls from confused travellers. (Supplied: Kathy Brown)

It is a similar story for Kathy Brown, owner of Wanaaring Store and Caravan Park, 230km east of Tibooburra, who said in the past few months the inaccuracies online have led to her getting hundreds of calls from confused drivers.

She said updates and emails from Transport NSW also differed from the electronic road condition signs and travellers were changing their plans because they believed certain roads were closed, with Google Maps, which uses Live Traffic NSW information, sending them on longer routes.

"It would be good if those that control Live Traffic NSW would actually check and make sure why the roads are closed or if it isn't," Ms Brown said.

Travellers left confused

Tony Bond from Yass has been trying to plan a trip to Cameron Corner, specifically from Wanaaring to Tibooburra, and up to Innamincka in South Australia, to support the struggling businesses who rely on tourism.

But he said the discrepancy between the Live Traffic NSW site and local reports had made it hard to plan.

"Some roads aren't even actually on [Live Traffic NSW] that we know are there for one, and they're saying they are not necessarily open when they are, and vice versa," Mr Bond said.

"We will look at those live sites anyway just in case there is something that's missed.

"But we pretty much rely these days on social media; on various groups like the Grey Nomads [Facebook page], various caravanning groups [and] four-wheel drive groups, because they are the people out there doing it, and [with] the roadhouses themselves, we will call ahead."

Grazier and president of the Pastoralists' Association of West Darling (PAWD) Sam Beven agreed, saying Live Traffic NSW was "problematic at best" and Transport NSW could do more to provide accurate information.

Sam Beven believes Transport NSW workers could be doing more to provide accurate information on road closures. (ABC Broken Hill: Katherine Spackman)

"I know there are a lot of roads in the unincorporated area [which are not managed by a local government], but whenever you see any roadworks getting done, there's a lot of people sitting in cars watching graters and watching loaders work," Mr Beven said.

"These people could maybe be driving around the district checking the roads so we can get a bit more [of an] accurate reading."

title: Cronulla coach's belief grows as Sharks surge towards NRL finals
text:
Cronulla is promising no let-up after extending its league-best winning streak to five matches, sparking talk that an elusive second NRL premiership is in the offing for the surging Sharks.

Rarely has understated coach Craig Fitzgibbon been more bullish about his belief in the team than after Sunday's dazzling 32-16 dispatch of South Sydney.

"I've never felt any different about the group in the last five years, to be honest, but maybe I believe in them more than they believe in themselves," he said.

With Nicho Hynes back to the vintage form that earned him the Dally M Medal and the Sharks a top-two finish in 2022, and his halves partner, Braydon Trindall, in career-best touch, the Sharks are flying with nine wins from their past 10 outings.

Michael Ennis, the club's 2016 grand final-winning hooker-turned-analyst, believes the Sharks will go all the way again a decade on from breaking the longest and most infamous title drought in premiership history.

It's 10 years since the Sharks beat the Storm in the NRL grand final and the club is shaping up to scale the heights again. (Getty Images: Mark Kolbe)

"We're working hard towards something and we've been building that for a little bit," Fitzgibbon said.

"And then sometimes you get things go your way, sometimes they don't. But at the moment, it's going our way.

"There's still plenty more. We'll have a hiccup here and there and there'll be turbulence, but you won't challenge me on how much I believe in them."

Sitting fourth and certain not to face any more top-eight opposition until the finals, the Sharks are well placed to snatch an all-important top-two spot.

But skipper Blayke Brailey says the Sharks won't be taking their foot off the pedal, with the side's immediate focus on Sunday's derby with St George Illawarra.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

The Dragons may be wooden spoon-bound but the Sharks won't be taking their arch rivals lightly, especially with points differential between the top teams looking increasingly important.

"A derby clash, no matter where you're sitting on the table, it's a tough contest," Brailey said.

"Those derby games are tough, no matter the form you're in."

After the Dragons at Kogarah, the Sharks face Canberra at home, the Titans on the Gold Coast, Parramatta away and Melbourne in a potentially crucial last-round battle at Shark Park.

AAP

title: Residents hope to raise $750,000 to fix small town's aged care problem
text:
Joan White and her husband Alan, affectionately known as Stumpy, did everything together.

They were side-by-side for 58 years of marriage, raising three sons and navigating the highs and lows of being primary producers on their Texas property on Queensland's southern border.

The former country mayor said she thinks euthanising 62 head of cattle rather than having them starve to death due to drought in 2015 was the beginning of the end for her husband.

Mr White soon developed dementia, and the couple sold their farm and moved to town in 2018 to be closer to care.

Joan and Stumpy White were married for 58 years and did everything together. (Supplied: Joan White)

"It became really, really horrendous," she said.

Ms White said her husband was sent to Millmerran, 120 kilometres away, to be cared for in an aged care facility after she had a heart attack.

"It is a sad story, but I don't want anybody else to make it their journey," she said.

In the small country town, there is no public transport and barely any traffic, but the number of mobility scooters used in the area highlights a big problem facing the aging community.

A sign outside the post office reads "Texas is a dementia friendly community" and features a picture of Mr and Ms White.

Joan and Stumpy White feature on a sign in the main street of Texas. (ABC Southern Qld: Elly Bradfield)

And while Texas has a median age of 53, 15 years higher than the rest of the country, it does not have an aged care facility.

Ms White is the driving force behind a community push to build a facility that could keep older people, including those with dementia, in their hometown.

The Texas Care Foundation Limited is a board of community members pulled together by the gaps in services for older people.

Joan and Alan are not alone

Brian and Annette Mearns have been married almost 60 years and fear being separated when they need aged care. (ABC Southern Qld: Elly Bradfield)

Aged care is a high priority for many of the town's 800 residents.

Brian Mearns, 83, and his wife Annette Mearns, 84, say they are on a "downhill run" both with serious health problems.

"I tell her she can leave anytime she likes, but I'm coming with her," Mr Mearns jokes.

"He's been telling me that for 60 years," she replies.

But the couple, who are due to celebrate their 60th anniversary in a few months, said the thought of being separated was "absolutely traumatic".

"You're used to someone in bed beside you at night and you're used to talking to someone at the table … and togetherness," Ms Mearns said.

They keep themselves busy tending to a beautiful garden, including 110 fruit trees, but accept there will be a time they will have to leave it behind.

They will likely move closer to family in Dalby, more than 200km away, but are supportive of the push for a local aged care facility.

Cristine Miller says she is worried about the future for her and her husband. (ABC Southern Qld: Elly Bradfield)

Cristine Miller, 75, and her 80-year-old husband were "taking each day at a time" but said they share the same worries.

"I just hope and pray I can look after Brian forever," she said.

" I tell him we've both got to die at home, but I haven't worked the time out yet. "

Sally-Ann Masters says she coped using humour during the hard years caring for her mother. (ABC Southern Qld: Elly Bradfield)

Sally-Ann Masters said dementia was her only fear in life after she saw her mother go from being a strong lady "back to being a little girl" when she was living with the condition.

"You grieve them twice. You grieve them while you're nursing them, and you grieve them when they've gone," she said.

Small community, big challenges

Rural GP Colin Owen has lived in the nearby town of Inglewood, 55km away, for 58 years, and has many patients from Texas.

He said in his opinion, home was the best place for people with dementia to be looked after.

But Dr Owen said when someone needs an aged care facility, it was best in the patient's hometown.

Residents in Texas say the idea of being separated to live in aged care is traumatic. (ABC Southern Qld: Elly Bradfield)

"This is where they grew up, this is where their family are, this is where they know people and my other belief is that they get looked after better in their own hometown by people who know them," he said.

Securing the site

Despite the challenges, Texas Care Foundation Limited has earmarked a 3.5-hectare property for an aged care home.

While Ms White said it would be a big task, but the group aims to raise $750,000 to secure the site in the next 12 months.

Board member Warwick Trim, the owner of a fuel supplier in town, said he felt it was his responsibility to become involved.

"We need something like this in Texas, not just now, but that will be for years and probably generations to come as well," he said.

"We're all going to get old one day."

When Joan White was awarded a Medal of the Order of Australia, Stumpy was too unwell to attend the official ceremony but they still celebrated together. (Supplied: Joan White)

Mr White said she would not stop until her big dream was a reality, motivated by her husband's memory.

She smiles when remembering Stumpy's final days, when she would climb into his hospital bed, and the nurses would say, "Look at these lovebirds".

"If he could touch my skin and I could rub his hand or rub his leg, he knew I was there," she said.

title: Single mum has front-row seat to first home buyer struggles
text:
It is a sunny Thursday afternoon in the leafy inner-city Perth suburb of Mount Hawthorn.

Tess McKenna is preparing afternoon tea for her four kids after getting home from a busy day at work.

Tess McKenna has four children aged under 13. (ABC News: Courtney Withers)

The 31-year-old gets them settled with some colouring-in at the dining table. Then she starts scrolling.

Ms McKenna works as a buyer's agent. (ABC News: Courtney Withers)

"It's really hard, it's a really hard market," she said.

" As a single parent I feel like right now it's very next to impossible for me. "

There is a limited number of affordable homes available in Perth. (ABC News: Courtney Withers)

She is on the hunt for an affordable first home in Perth — something well under $1 million, in a good, established area with space for the kids.

But she is not alone in that search. She is just one of thousands competing in a market described by experts as "messy", "unaffordable" and "very limited".

Familiar with disappointment

Ms McKenna understands Perth property well because she analyses it for a living.

Working as a buyer's agent, a role increasingly sought by first home buyers to help with their search, she is in tune with the current challenges.

Ms McKenna is well-versed in the challenges faced by first home buyers. (ABC News: Courtney Withers)

She knows all too well the feeling of scrolling websites only to be disappointed the next day when listings are marked sold.

She relates to the stress of searching for properties while going from rental to rental as cost of living pressures rise.

"It's very isolating, and there are not many options," she said.

"You feel like you're going backwards and you're constantly having all this self-doubt thinking that you're failing."

The McKenna family is competing with thousands of others in a tough market. (ABC News: Courtney Withers)

She has made her current rental feel like home with art on the wall and photos lining the fridge, but the last few years have not been easy.

"A lot of the time I'm left living pay cheque to pay cheque and month by month … and I'm having to dip into any savings that I potentially might have been able to put towards [a] deposit," she said.

"It just seems to get harder."

Advised to shop around

The buyer's agent first started looking for a property two-and-a-half years ago. Since 2023, she has lived in four rentals.

The irony of helping others with the same problem she is facing is not lost on Ms McKenna.

"The Australian dream is to own a home, so when it seems so out of reach for people and so impossible, I definitely can relate," she said.

"The fact that I can help other people do it [find a home] is awesome. I would love to do it for myself."

Tess McKenna helps others to find homes, but would love to achieve that for herself too. (ABC News: Courtney Withers)

She said houses around the $600,000-mark close to the city have become almost non-existent, likely because Perth's median house price is still stubbornly high after breaking through the $1 million mark in January.

Property analyst Gavin Hegney said he is now advising first home buyers in Perth to hold off and shop around.

Gavin Hegney is a real estate expert, property valuer and advisor. (ABC News: Courtney Withers)

"If a normal cycle prevails we should see a settling back in values over the next 12 months," he said.

"Prices are coming off a bit in some areas, and so there's no sense of urgency.

"It creates a little bit of uncertainty for first home buyers wondering whether they should be paying prices of today or whether the price will be cheaper in a year's time."

Perth no longer 'affordable state'

Curtin University property professor Steven Rowley said Perth's property squeeze had been driven by one factor.

Steven Rowley is the director of the Australian Housing and Urban Research Institute’s Curtin Research Centre. (ABC News: Courtney Withers)

"We've had really strong demand, particularly from investors the last few years, and there just isn't the supply there," he said.

"[The] combination of a really struggling rental market plus very strong demand and low supply in the buying market has meant real problems for first home buyers."

Perth's median house price surges through $1 milion mark Domain's latest quarterly house price report has found the cost to buy a home increased by 9.9 per cent in the last quarter of 2025, to a median of $1,087,762.

He said while Perth used to be considered "the affordable state" that is "no longer the case", pointing to substantial growth at the bottom end of the market.

"We've caught up with Melbourne, we're not that far behind Sydney, we've accelerated ahead of Adelaide … because of that demand-supply balance," he said.

He said some "generous government schemes" probably have not helped in terms of inflating prices — namely, the Help to Buy Scheme, the 5 per cent Deposit Scheme and WA's Keystart program.

Property analyst Mr Hegney also believes the federal government's negative gearing tax changes in this year's budget are not necessarily helping.

"We've got two investors walking out [of the market] for every one first home buyer walking in. The problem is not all first home buyers are in a position to be able to buy today," he said.

Laser focus on supply

WA Housing Minister John Carey said he has a "resolute focus" on getting more supply onto the market.

"As a government you keep making bold decisions," he said.

"I accept that some of the decisions I'm making, particularly around enabling 50,000 subdivisions, do not resonate [with everyone]."

John Carey says he is determined to bring more property supply to market. (ABC News: Courtney Withers)

Referencing proposed building code subdivision changes announced last month, Mr Carey said "more medium density" was needed in WA.

"We're not taking [the West Australian] dream away from people, but what we are trying to do is create choice for young couples, first-home buyers who might actually want to buy an apartment that's well-serviced, close to a public train station," he said.

When asked when it would get easier for first home buyers, Mr Carey said he "can't anticipate the future".

"There isn't a single silver bullet, but by god we've got to keep pushing out that housing and introducing new measures, new reforms, cutting red tape — whatever it takes," he said.

Cold comfort

For Ms McKenna it is cold comfort as she continues her search.

She has not given up hope completely, but the constant scrolling and missing out has worn her down.

"I definitely do feel a bit defeated at times," she said.

Ms McKenna says she still has hope and will secure a place. (ABC News: Courtney Withers)

"I still hold hope that I will get there and I'm sure I will. I'm quite a determined person.

"At some stage there has to be some sort of change that'll happen to make it possible."

title: Port guide: Palermo, Italy
text:
