The arrivals were equivalent to nearly two-thirds of Ceuta's permanent population of about 83,000.

How and why did the migrants enter?

Ceuta and Melilla, another Spanish exclave on the North African coast, are the only two land borders between the European Union and Africa.

Many arrivals swam to Ceuta around the Tarajal breakwater — a sea wall extending out from the Spain-Morocco border into the Mediterranean — to come ashore at Tarajal beach.

READ MORE The Spanish territory at the centre of a unique migration challenge

"Spain gives you the chance to make your future, not like Morocco," Buji, a 21-year-old Moroccan who is studying to be a teacher, told the Associated Press (AP). "I am a talented boy. I just want a chance."

He said he lost his belongings and money in the crossing, and when he realised that he would likely face legal limbo and detention, he turned back.

"I’ve spent perhaps 14 years studying, but there’s nothing at home, and I'd have to work 12-hour shifts for a meagre wage," he told AP.

"That’s why I came here, but I haven’t found any opportunities here either, so I have to go back."

To reach the city, migrants have been known to swim around 5km from the Moroccan town of Fnideq.

Officials said at least 67 bodies were recovered on the Spanish side after some migrants drowned and others were crushed while trying to climb the breakwater and border fence.

Many were driven to migrate by economic hardship and reportedly by rumours circulating on Moroccan social media that border security had been relaxed.

Spanish interior minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska blamed people-smuggling networks for exploiting vulnerable migrants by spreading misleading interpretations of a recent Spanish Supreme Court ruling.

Spain's immigration policies

Spain's 29 June Supreme Court ruling said authorities cannot summarily deport migrants who arrive by sea without due process, because they did not cross the physical border barriers referenced in Spanish law.

Gemma Pinyol-Jiménez, head of migration policies and diversity at Instrategies and an associate researcher at GRITIM–Pompeu Fabra University, told CNN that it effectively means migrants can't be pushed back at sea because there is no crossing of a formal border.

It does not mean people cannot be sent back, and the deportation process can still be completed within days.

"The idea is to facilitate the work of the police, but it doesn’t mean these people can stay in Ceuta," she said.

In contrast to much of Europe, Spain has adopted a less restrictive stance on migrants, introducing a program to grant residency to more than half a million undocumented people already living there.

Experts have said that summer sea conditions, Spain's relatively strong economy, and its immigration policies may have contributed to the surge in migrant arrivals.

How have world leaders responded?

The mass crossing triggered alarm across the European Union.

Leaders of Italy, Denmark, Austria, Belgium, Bulgaria, Cyprus, Croatia, the Czech Republic, Estonia, Finland, Germany, Greece, Hungary, Latvia, Lithuania, Malta, the Netherlands, Poland, Romania, Slovenia, Slovakia and Sweden signed a letter asking the EU’s current Irish presidency to convene a video conference of interior ministers.

"We cannot allow uncontrolled mass crossings, the instrumentalisation of migration or other hybrid threats to create the perception that illegal entry into the European Union is possible. That a migrant’s illegal entry can turn into legal stay," the letter said.

The meeting has been scheduled for Tuesday.

Italy announced on Friday it was suspending its Schengen arrangements with Spain for a month in response to the incident.

The Schengen agreement allows passport-free travel between 29 European countries.

Thousands of migrants crossed from Morocco into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta in north Africa, many of them by swimming. Source: Getty / Marcos Moreno

"This is an extraordinary measure, adopted to safeguard national security and prevent possible repercussions for our nation," Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, a right-wing leader who campaigned on a pledge to reduce illegal immigration, wrote on X.

Italy, which does not share a land border with Spain, also said it had agreed with France to strengthen controls along their border to try to prevent undocumented migrants from crossing.

Spain's centre-left prime minister, Pedro Sanchez, criticised the decision as "selfish, polarising and unlawful".

United States President Donald Trump, whose mass immigration crackdowns have been a key pillar of his second term, held a cabinet meeting about what he called a "catastrophe" and what "looks like an invasion" in Spain.

"That same thing is going to happen to us if the Republicans don’t get elected," he said.

Dozens of people died while attempting to cross into Ceuta. Source: Getty / Europa Press News

Spain said migrants who entered Ceuta irregularly would not be allowed to travel onwards to mainland Spain or elsewhere in the Schengen area.

It said order had been restored within 24 hours and that reinforced police and military deployments would remain for as long as necessary.

Migrants return

Hundreds of migrants continued to make their way back to Morocco on Saturday, some saying they had done so voluntarily, leaving Ceuta after what they described as degrading treatment on the Spanish side of the border.

They walked along a long stretch of beach before slipping into Morocco through a small breach in the border fence.

"I decided to come back on my own," Ouail Lamzeiz told AP.

"I spent eight days in Ceuta, and I was about to get a bed at the migrant centre, but I hadn’t eaten for days. Even the Moroccans there didn't help."

Migrants told AP they spent their nights sleeping in the forests around Ceuta because they could not find shelter, and that they often fought over food.

Others have said they do not intend to return.

Mohamed Hatri, a 23-year-old Moroccan, said he was determined to stay.

"They've closed everything down so that we can’t buy anything to eat, to force us to return to our country," he told AP.

title: 'Never bring a knife to a gunfight': The next frontier in online security
text:
In brief Both OpenAI and Anthropic have revealed in recent days that their models autonomously hacked other organisations.

An AI cybersecurity expert says organisations must now arm themselves with "the ability to react at the same machine speed that the AI would have".

Recent incidents involving some of the world's most advanced artificial intelligence companies have exposed emerging challenges in an increasingly complex cybersecurity landscape.

This week, Anthropic, the AI company behind the digital assistant Claude, said its AI models compromised real-world systems belonging to three other organisations during internal testing, compromising their infrastructure by exploiting weak passwords and other basic techniques.

The company said it had discovered the incidents after launching a review in response to an announcement days earlier by OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT.

OpenAI recently revealed that one of its models had broken free from its virtual testing environment and hacked another tech company, Hugging Face.

Germaine Tan Shu Ting, vice president of security and AI at AI cybersecurity platform DarkTrace, told SBS News these developments were "very concerning".

"The big question that we have in the back of our head is: if these incidents are happening to the likes of OpenAI and Anthropic, what's to say that's not happening to other data systems, other AI systems in the world?" she said.

"The answer is: We will never know."

Tan Shu Ting said that the fact both companies had publicly disclosed the incidents was reassuring, but it underscored the need for organisations to shield themselves against increasingly autonomous systems that can operate at unprecedented pace.

How can organisations protect themselves?

Tan Shu Ting said companies must get the basics right, be prepared, and have systems in place to detect anomalies and AI threats.

"Get control of your data. Basic cyber-hygiene. Get visibility of what you have, and then arm yourselves with the ability to react at the same machine speed that the AI would have," she said.

"So they would say, never bring a knife to a gunfight, and I think it's very relevant here.

"You need to be able to act as fast as these AI systems. So how do you set yourself up for those situations?"

Regulations will also provide an important layer of safety, she said — but many experts have flagged concerns that legislative protections are not keeping pace with the rapid advances in AI.

The technology has been adopted by nearly 53 per cent of the world’s population in three years, faster than the spread of the PC or the internet, according to a study released this year by Stanford University.

"Before advanced AI agents are widely deployed, organisations need stronger containment, limited access, continuous monitoring, clear audit trails, reliable shutdown controls and independent safety testing," Walayat Hussain, head of the Information Technology and Systems discipline at the Australian Catholic University, said last week.

"The lesson is not that we should stop developing advanced AI, but that safety, governance and red teaming must develop just as quickly as the technology itself.”

The race to regulate

Last month, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese announced a plan to legislate a set of AI standards by early next year.

It is expected to address education and training, workplace rights and productivity, and a plan to fast-track data-centre approvals to attract investment in Australia.

Countries around the world are racing to implement better AI legislation, with these latest incidents amplifying pressure from officials in the US and Europe for greater government oversight of AI companies.

"We're looking at controls," US President Donald Trump told reporters on Thursday.

The European Commission said it had been briefed by OpenAI and Anthropic over the hacking incidents.

Europe's AI Act, which comes into force on Sunday, is one of the most aggressive regulations the high-tech sector has faced so far, as fears rise over the risks AI poses to society.

Under the act, AI companies will be required to make clear to consumers, through labels or digital watermarks, that chatbots or imagery are generated with AI.

The European Commission said in a statement that new regulations also aim to address "systemic risks" posed by AI like "chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear incidents, loss of control, cyber offense, harmful manipulation and threats to fundamental rights".

Failure to comply could result in fines of millions of Euros or a percentage of the company's global turnover.

title: 'Mirage': Voice architect Noel Pearson breaks silence at Garma on referendum defeat
text:
In brief Noel Pearson addressed Garma Festival on Saturday, his first major public speech since the Voice to Parliament referendum was defeated in 2023.

Pearson, co-founder of the Cape York Land Council, was one of the Voice's architects.

Noel Pearson, the architect of the failed Voice to Parliament 2023 referendum, has given his first major public speech in three years at this year's Garma Festival, Australia's largest Indigenous cultural gathering.

"For those of us who urged faith, hope and love, there is an account to be given for the hopes raised, the faith urged and the love lost in the referendum," he said.

"I must account for that. Three years later, I stand here with great reluctance.

"What right has anyone to raise hopes when those hopes were so badly misplaced? What right has anyone to offer a vision that turns out to be a mirage? That is the source of my hesitation to speak of these things. But I cannot allow the failure of the referendum to excuse me from my responsibility."

Nearly three years have passed since just over 60 per cent of Australians voted against enshrining an Indigenous Voice in the constitution, with every state and territory except the ACT rejecting the proposal.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Pearson, co-founder of the Cape York Land Council, was a prominent "Yes" campaigner at the time.

In his speech on Gumatj Country in the Northern Territory, he showed a map of where the majority of voters voted yes or no, with "blue dots" showing locations voting in favour of the referendum.

Blue dots represent the communities where a majority voted yes for the Voice to Parliament, while red dots represent a majority no vote. Credit: Australian Electoral Commission

"The discrete Indigenous communities of Australia, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander, overwhelmingly wanted the Voice. The rest of the country did not," he said.

"I come from one of these blue dot places.

"Fifty kilometres from my blue-dot home is the orange-dot township of Cooktown. Captain Cook spent six weeks there in 1770. I was born in its hospital. In 2023, Cook's town voted 'no'."

'Our present is not good'

According to an estimate by political analyst Simon Jackman, in areas where Indigenous Australians made up the majority of the population, 63 per cent voted "Yes".

"From the very beginning of my public life, it was, and still is, the future of those communities, not least my own, that has been the central focus of my wakeful dreams," Pearson said.

READ MORE A remote corner of Australia is about to swell for a major gathering

"Our present is not good. And nor is our future assured. The things that worried me when I was 22 now distress me at 61.

"When I was 22, I worried because we knew something needed to be done, but we did not yet know how to do it. Now, we are much clearer. We know what we need to do. We know what we want to do."

Calls to dismantle state Aboriginal Affairs departments

Pearson added the "blue dot communities", communities voted in favour of the referendum, "stand in grave need of healing".

"There is no better solution to healing individuals, families and communities than guaranteed work," he said.

"They will start to heal. They will start to grow. They will start to strengthen.

"Every child in these blue-dot communities needs to be guaranteed an education."

According to the latest data from the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS), in 2022 9.5 per cent of First Nations people aged between 15 and 64 were unemployed.

Pearson said that "the blue-dot communities of remote Australia must become the sole jurisdiction of the Commonwealth".

Noel Pearson was one of the most outspoken proponents for the Yes campaign during the Voice to Parliament referendum. Source: AAP / James Ross

"These communities and their lands would still come under the shared jurisdiction of the relevant states and territories for most functions governed by the state’s constitutional responsibilities, but the administrative relationship for Aboriginal affairs would lie with the Commonwealth," he said.

"There should be no need for Aboriginal Affairs departments in the states and territories."

Pearson added that "a direct funding relationship between the Commonwealth and the organisations representing and serving these blue-dot communities will enable development agendas ... to receive the budgetary support it needs to close the gap."

"After the rejection of the Voice, the conversation about structural reform of the federal arrangements governing indigenous affairs must resume," he said.

'Not a monoculture country'

Foreign Minister Penny Wong, one of the other speakers at Garma on Saturday, also began her speech by reflecting on the festival's theme, 'Bukmak' — meaning 'Everyone'.

"Bukmak is a powerful message at this time for our country, to all of us. A powerful message about who we are, where we have come from, and most importantly, where we want to go as a country," she said.

"At a time when there are those who seek to set us apart, First Nations peoples, with your generosity, remind us how many different stories brought together make us stronger."

"No matter your background, no matter your culture, your race, your religion, or your language. Garma is an invitation to everyone to come together, to learn together," Wong said. Source: AAP / James Ross

Wong has attended the festival this year instead of Prime Minister Albanese, whose absence from the festival has drawn some criticism. The prime minister has defended the decision, saying he hasn't "[had] a day off all year" and noting that he has attended each year since 2019.

Wong made veiled criticism of One Nation leader Pauline Hanson, who has been advocating for a "monocultural" Australia, without directly naming her or her party.

READ MORE Two years on from the Voice referendum, its architects remain committed to the cause

"As I look around here at this festival, this is who we are. So rich in history, so rich in culture, home to more than 300 ancestries, and we share common ground with so many of the world's peoples," Wong said.

"We are not a monoculture, and we have never been. And this is why we want to bring more of who we are to our foreign policy."

'Some really difficult challenges'

Minister for Indigenous Australians Malarndirri McCarthy was also among the governmental figures at the festival, highlighting issues Indigenous Australians are facing.

"We've had our disappointments. There's no two ways about that. And there are still some really difficult challenges, really tough challenges," she said.

"Those high rates of incarceration. Our state and territory governments across Australia need to recognise how much that really hurts our people and suffocates the ability to grow strong in this country."

The ABS reports that more than 17,000 Aboriginals and Torres Strait Islanders are incarcerated, accounting for one-third of the nation's prisoners.

title: FIFA abandons World Cup privatisation plan after fierce backlash
text:
In brief FIFA planned to create a commercial subsidiary that would run its main events, including the World Cup, which private investors could buy stakes in.

FIFA president Gianni Infantino announced on Saturday the plan was being scrapped.

FIFA has abandoned plans to sell a stake in the World Cup after fierce backlash, including threats of boycotts.

In a statement on Saturday morning, FIFA president Gianni Infantino said it had "become clear that the project has created divisions of a nature that, regardless of the level of support, are no longer in the interest of the objective set out in the first place".

"Our purpose has always been — and will always be — to unite and improve," he said.

"As a result, this proposal will not proceed.

"Moving forward, my intent is to bring all interested parties back together in the coming days and weeks in the spirit of shared interest in our game, and with the objective to continue growing football everywhere, particularly in those countries that mostly need our support."

FIFA on Wednesday announced its plan to create a commercial subsidiary known as the FIFA Forward Enterprise that would run its main events, including the World Cup.

Private investors would have been able to buy a minority stake of up to 20 per cent in the subsidiary, which was valued up to US$20 billion ($28.47 billion).

FIFA had promised each of its 211 member countries and territories US$40 million ($56.9 million) in funding for the 2027-2030 cycle if they agreed to the plan.

READ MORE The $28 billion plan at the centre of a growing FIFA storm

But the backlash to the proposal was fierce, with the 55 member states of the European football governing body UEFA voting unanimously to boycott all FIFA tournaments.

Other bodies also opposed the plan, including CONCACAF, the regional federation for North America, Central America and the Caribbean, as did the Asian Football Confederation, of which Australia is a part of.

The plan also exposed internal division within FIFA.

Infantino's senior adviser Carlos Cordeiro resigned and called the plan a "bad deal for football", while FIFA chief operating officer Kevin Lamour said staff had been "deceived" by Infantino and the proposal was a "project of one person".

InspirationCruises Port guide: Palermo, Italy Brian Johnston August 3, 2026 — 1:27pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

This article is part of Traveller’s ultimate guide to cruise ports. See all stories .

The capital of Sicily was once avoided thanks to its grime and Mafia connections but has cleaned up its act and become Italy’s latest tourist hotspot. Tourism in Palermo is booming. iStock Who goes there Thanks to several superb monuments and art museums, very lively street life, great food and the world’s best gelato, tourism in Palermo is booming and more cruise ships are visiting than ever before, with the season extending into winter. All the big cruise lines sail there, so do many smaller ones, usually on Italian or western Mediterranean itineraries, but sometimes on longer voyages from starting points such as Southampton. Sail on in

Advertisement

Don’t get too excited. The backing of mountains is nice, but Palermo itself is mostly flat and doesn’t reveal much by way of charm on the approach. To starboard looms Monte Pellegrino, a lumpy peninsula inhabited since Palaeolithic times. Its Sanctuary of Saint Rosalia is a pilgrim site. Sign up for the Traveller Deals newsletter Get exclusive travel deals delivered straight to your inbox. Sign up now. Berth rites No surprises at the Stazione Marittima: a white cruise terminal recently renovated, berths for several ships, a tourist information office and other basic facilities. You’re well-positioned for visiting the city, but head inland rather than be tempted by the waterfront, which is flanked by a busy road. Beware taxi drivers unless you want to be fleeced. Going ashore If you’re a hearty walker, you could see almost everything on foot but otherwise use the hop-on hop-off bus. Top sights are the Palazzo dei Normanni and especially its staggering chapel covered in glittering Byzantine-style mosaic work, La Martorana church, the cathedral, and the Galleria Regionale for medieval artworks. However, this city of crumbling, blackened baroque buildings provides interesting architecture at every turn, as well as street markets, lively back alleys and hidden chapels bursting with baroque encrustations.

Advertisement

Don’t miss Although it isn’t in Palermo but 10 kilometres outside it, Monreale Cathedral is one of Sicily’s top sights. A 12th-century Byzantine-Arab-Norman architectural fusion created one of medieval Europe’s great buildings. Floors are inlaid with coloured jasper and porphyry, wooden ceilings are patterned in green and gold, and walls and ceilings covered with dazzling Byzantine mosaics showing biblical scenes, from Noah clambering off his ark to Lazarus being unwrapped by amazed onlookers. The cloister is distinctly Islamic in style, with formal gardens, columned arcades and a fountain strikingly like those in Spain’s Alhambra Palace. Get active The alternatively traffic-choked or narrow pedestrianised streets of Palermo aren’t conducive to running or cycling and, while the nearby Madonie mountains are good for hiking and mountain biking, they aren’t easy to get to in a cruise day. Use the ship’s gym instead. Best bites

Advertisement

Lay off the four-course meals on the ship and save stomach space for snacking in Palermo because Sicilian food is a splendid explosion of flavours that draws on its amazing cultural heritage from Asia Minor, North Africa, Greece, Spain and Italy. You’ll want to try arancini, sfinciuni (the local pizza), pannelle (chickpea fritters) and cannoli for a start. Pani ca meusa (spleen sandwich, a street-market speciality) is better than it sounds. For something more substantial, tuck into pasta con le sarde, pasta with sardines, saffron, pine nuts and raisins. Further afield You have several very fine options that will set you dithering, including Monreale cathedral, Segesta for its superb Greek temple in a country setting, Cefalu for its old town and beaches, and cliff-clinging Erice for medieval streets and fabulous views. Agrigento, which has several Greek temples, is another option but the drive is two hours each way, and the site will be hot and crowded by the time you get there, so best reconsider unless you’re a ruin fanatic.

The Australian sharemarket has slid lower at the open with heavier losses averted after US President Donald Trump said on Sunday he’s holding off on delivering new strikes on Iran, while the US confirmed. The S&P/ASX 200 was down 29.8 points, or 0.3 per cent, in early trade, with 10 of 11 industry sectors in negative territory, with only utilities in the green. Futures had predicted a loss of more than 1 per cent, but they were set on Saturday before Trump backed down after Tehran and other Middle Eastern powers told him they’re working on an agreement that might quickly reopen the Strait of Hormuz. Wall Street closed a losing month with gains on Friday. Bloomberg Elsewhere, the US dollar weakened sharply against the Japanese yen after Trump and Japan’s finance minister confirmed both sides had intervened in markets. The yen’s prolonged weakness against the dollar has been a source of frustration for Tokyo. Since Japan imports so much of what it consumes, a weak currency pushes prices higher, increasing inflation.

When asked why Washington was helping, Trump said on Sunday (US time) that “We have a good relationship with Japan. We’re very strong - very, very strong financially - and they are, you know, they have a weakening yen, and they wanted a little bit of help, and we’re always there for Japan. Japan’s been very good to us, with the exception, of course, of Pearl Harbour.” Trump said the US got “financial benefit” out of the intervention, calling it a “signal of friendship.” “It’s also good for the world economy.” Trump said he’d agreed to cancel the attack, “subject to being able to rapidly make a DEAL” to quickly reopen the Strait of Hormuz, according to a post on Truth Social. “Get to work, everybody, and get it DONE.” The latest developments sent oil prices falling, with Brent, the international standard, shedding 4.6 per cent and WTI oil for September falling 4.7 per cent in early Asian trade. Energy stocks lost ground in early trade, with Woodside and Santos each shedding 1.5 per cent. Mining stocks are mixed with BHP edging up 0.1 per cent while Rio Tinto dipped 0.1 per cent and Fortescue fell 1.9 per cent. Gold miners are mixed too, with Northern Star losing 0.5 per cent and Evolution Mining adding 1 per cent.

The Australian dollar was trading at US70.42¢ at 10.07am AEST. On Wall Street on Friday, the S&P 500 climbed 0.7 per cent after veering between gains and losses through the day. It’s a fitting finish to July for the US stock market, which lurched up and down as oil prices shot higher because of the war with Iran and worries grew about whether Big Tech’s massive investments in artificial-intelligence technology will translate into profits and whether chipmaker stocks soared too high in the euphoria around AI. Friday’s gains sent the S&P 500 to its first winning week in three, but the main measure of the US stock market nevertheless finished the month with a tiny loss. Amazon led the market with a leap of 15.3 per cent after reporting much stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected. Its profit more than tripled from a year earlier, thanks in part to an acceleration of growth in its cloud computing business. Analysts said that could be a signal Amazon’s huge AI investments are paying off, and Amazon increased its forecast for how much it will spend on investments this year. The reaction was similar to what Microsoft got a day before, when its stock soared to its best day in nearly 18 years on signals that its AI investments may also be yielding higher profits.

Chip companies selling the processors and computer memory that such “hyperscalers” are scrambling to buy swung sharply again on Friday. Micron Technology, for example, went from an early jump of 6.4 per cent to a loss of 6.5 per cent before finishing with a fall of 5.9 per cent. More firmly on the losing end of Wall Street was Apple, which dropped 7.4 per cent despite reporting stronger profit for the latest quarter than expected. Its forecast for revenue growth in the current quarter fell short of expectations, which executives pinned on a supply crunch in components getting vacuumed up in the AI boom. Meanwhile, a selloff in US Treasuries last week signalled the need for the Federal Reserve to earn its inflation-fighting “credibility” with interest rate increases, St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem told the Financial Times. “At this juncture, earlier, incremental, gradual interest-rate action is preferable, less costly and less disruptive than potentially later, larger and abrupt actions,” Musalem, who is not a voting member of the Federal Open Market Committee this year, told the FT. Musalem, who sits on the rate-setting body, told the newspaper he had “expressed a preference” towards a quarter-percentage-point interest rate increase at this week’s policy meeting, where the Fed left rates unchanged.

Warsh has told financial markets that he does not want to give hints about what the Fed will do with interest rates, saying he wants to get direct, “unfiltered” messages from them rather than echoes back of what the Fed has suggested. But “without clarifying why action was or wasn’t taken already, it’s hard to see how statements about being committed to hitting its inflation target aren’t just a bluff,” according to Brian Jacobsen, chief economic strategist at Annex Wealth Management. “The Fed is facing a growing credibility problem,” economists at Bank of America wrote in a report. NSW and Sydney Roosters assistant Matt King will take over as the Blues’ State of Origin coach following Laurie Daley’s decision earlier on Monday to stand aside. King was Daley’s senior assistant as NSW captured the interstate series against the odds this year with a famous victory in game three at Suncorp Stadium. Matt King is set to be given a two-year deal as NSW’s Origin coach. NRL Photos The former Blues outside back was Daley’s favoured successor and has also won over top brass at the NSW Rugby League. Sources not authorised to speak publicly on the matter confirmed the news on Monday. King, who previously worked on Michael Maguire’s coaching staff at South Sydney, has been with the Roosters for a decade and is regarded as a future NRL head coach. He played nine Origins for NSW and won 10 Kangaroos caps in a playing career that took in stints at Melbourne and South Sydney, and Warrington in the Super league.

Advertisement

It is expected he will be handed a two-year contract with NSW. It is unclear if King will continue full-time with the Roosters next season, but there is no rule against being an assistant at club level and an Origin coach at the same time. Loading Daley gave his endorsement to the 45-year-old after saying it was “just the right time” to walk away from the NSW post. As reported by this masthead on Sunday afternoon, Daley confirmed on Monday morning via his Sky Sports Radio Big Sports Breakfast program that he would not renew his Origin deal.

Advertisement

He had been frustrated last week by a News Corp report that he had quit due to health concerns, which he quickly denied – but only after several family members had become concerned and contacted him. Daley was glad he got to bow out with a series win that was sealed with a victory on Queensland soil. Blues head coach Laurie Daley (right) speaks to his assistant Matt King (left). Getty “I feel like now is the right time for someone else to have the opportunity to lead this great state and this great team,” Daley said. “It’s just the right time. “You always have to be careful that you don’t make decisions based on emotion. You have to think things through. When we won game three, you sit back, reflect, which is why I didn’t want to make the announcement straight away.

“Over the last couple of weeks, from where I was going into the series to where I was after the game, it hadn’t changed. I knew my commitment to the team was for that two-year period. “I felt like it was the best time to leave – it was the best time to pass the baton onto someone else.” Laurie Daley’s time as NSW Blues coach is over. title: ‘What drugs do you want?’ How betting companies lured Luke Bateman into gambling more
text:
Advertisement

PoliticsFederalGambling ‘What drugs do you want?’ How betting companies lured Luke Bateman into gambling more Natassia Chrysanthos Updated August 3, 2026 — 12:29pm ,first published 12:01pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Former rugby league player turned BookTok influencer Luke Bateman has described being flown to interstate race days by betting companies, where he was plied with alcohol and supplied with his choice of drugs, including in the presence of senior gambling company executives. As he told a Senate inquiry about the tactics betting companies used to induce him into gambling more money, Bateman said he would also steal from his mother, partner and siblings so he could redeem the $1000 worth of free bonus bets that he would be offered after losing everything. Luke Bateman during a hearing into Labor’s gambling bill. Alex Ellinghausen “The inducements really destroyed my life because that’s what kept you coming back... when you wanted to get out,” Bateman said. “But it also destroyed the lives of the people who loved me as well.” The 31-year-old was one in a lineup of gambling reform advocates, including former Victorian MP Russell Northe, who outlined how they were wooed by betting companies while in the depths of addiction. Star Casino, Tabcorp and SportsBet were named in witness testimony about gamblers being offered free hotel rooms, escorts, drugs and grand final tickets as part of “VIP” programs.

Advertisement

The Albanese government’s contentious gambling package does not ban betting inducements, despite full prohibition being recommended by the Murphy report in 2023. Related Article Good Weekend How Luke Bateman became Australia’s most unlikely book influencer “On Wednesdays and Saturdays, which are your two main race days, I would receive direct offers customised for me that basically said if you deposit $1000, we will give you $1000 in bonus bets,” Bateman said on Monday, saying those messages came through text messages and emails. “Even if you didn’t put on a bet for one weekend, the next Wednesday and Friday, you would receive those promotions and inducements once again ... directly targeted, to motivate you into gambling.” Asked by ACT Senator David Pocock to describe the most “gobsmacking examples” of inducements, Bateman said: “There were times where I would be flown interstate and taken to race days, put in marquees with alcohol and food provided all day, things like that.

Advertisement

“Before getting there, the VIP manager would offer: hey mate, what drugs do you want? Do you want a couple of bags for this weekend? We’ll organise that for you. We’ll have that ready for you when you get here.” Another time, Bateman said he was hosted at an exclusive event on the canals of the Gold Coast. Loading “And the entire C-suite of the company was there. All the management team administration, and they were all in a backroom doing drugs together. And I was out in this room doing drugs with all of them. This is like the CEO, the founders, the VIP managers,” he said. “I would have been, you know, 23 years old. So while I was absolutely ... I would put my hand up and say I was a willing participant of that. These are men in positions of power with influence who should be looking out for your welfare.”

Advertisement

Asked whether the presence of C-suite executives meant these companies knew how the system worked, Bateman said: “Well, not only did they know, they were participating in it.” Luke Bateman in 2017, during his time as an NRL player. Getty Images Bateman said there were many times when his gambling was extremely erratic, and showed signs of extreme harm – turning over hundreds of thousands of dollars in a single day, on hundreds of races. But there were never any welfare checks. Instead, companies drew him in further. Bateman has previously described being in hundreds of thousands of dollars of debt and unable to buy groceries. Star Casino, TAB, Sportsbet named in evidence A bipartisan report helmed by the late Peta Murphy in 2023 had recommended a total gambling advertising blackout, ban on inducements and national regulator. The witnesses to Monday morning said these were glaring omissions in Labor’s final legislation.

Advertisement

Chief gambling advocate Tim Costello said Prime Minister Anthony Albanese had set himself three tests with this gambling legislation: to delink gambling and sport, protect children and reduce the saturation of gambling ads. “We think this legislation in its present form fails those tests,” he said. “This legislation has some good aspects ... However, it’s line ball whether it’s actually better than the status quo.” Costello shared the story of one man who would soon plead guilty to criminal offences – a financial adviser who stole $12.3 million from his company in 17 months. “In that time, he was given free accommodation at Star Casino. He had to leave each week so they could technically say he wasn’t living there and come back the next morning,” Costello said. “He was the TAB’s biggest customer in that time. They were giving him $50,000 bonus bets. He was also Sportsbet’s biggest customer. They were flying him to grand finals. They were offering him escorts, drugs, whatever he wanted. He was doing turnover of more than $20 million a month.”

Advertisement

Costello said the question for the inquiry was: “How do licensed bookmakers, who we are told are regulated, get away with this? The answer is the first recommendation of the Murphy report. We don’t have a national regulator – that’s how they’re getting away with this.” Northe also pleaded with the inquiry to consider a national regulator. His own political career collapsed under the weight of gambling addiction – he served a year in prison after the Victorian County Court heard he falsely claimed more than $170,000 in parliamentary expenses during 2018 and 2019, while losing more than $223,000 through gambling over the same period. Related Article Exclusive

Gambling Labor’s millions in gambling donations revealed amid last-ditch push for reform “From my own experience, what happened to me quite regularly was I would open and close accounts on a regular basis, and that was a cry for help for me – closing an account, trying to get out,” he told the inquiry. “But during that period where I was stopped gambling and I had closed an account, I would be targeted, contacted by the gambling companies to reopen [an] account again with inducements and incentives.

Advertisement

“Recommendation 16 of the Murphy report: it says to ban inducements without delay. Here we are what 1132 days down the track and it’s still happening. What carnage has been caused in that time?” Another advocate, Mark Kempster, said he was working with one family who had lost $500,000 in 30 days after being given $55,000 worth of bonus bets – the person had been allowed on a betting app in one part of the country, despite being self-excluded in another. “Those types of things that happen across nearly all the major VIP programs that I’ve seen,” he said. TAB and Responsible Wagering Australia, the peak body for gambling companies, have been contacted for comment. Both Albanese and Communications Minister Anika Wells have defended the package, saying it is stronger than current settings.

Advertisement

Wells on Monday addressed the issue of inducements by saying people could sign up to the self-exclusion register, BetStop. Latest data shows 40,000 people had active exclusions with BetStop as of June; advocates say about 2 million Australians are at risk. “I would say to people who are either suffering from gambling harm or … who have been advocating in the space of inducements, to assist the cause by making sure that people who might benefit from BetStop are aware of BetStop,” Wells told reporters in Canberra. Albanese said last month. “I think we’ve got the balance right … It actually, in some ways, goes further than [the Murphy] report went. It’s a comprehensive approach.” Related Article Gambling ‘How can it be?’ Church leader turns Albanese’s words against him Witness Kate Seselja was brought to tears as she described her frustration at Albanese’s insistence that the government’s legislation had gotten “the balance right”.

Advertisement

“It just was so horrible to hear him say those words when there is absolutely no balance to this equation,” she said. “The stories of people harmed by this industry: when is enough? Like when is it enough? How many of us have to line up and say this is not okay?” Another advocate, Anne Bardsley, said it was “beyond frustrating” to know that the government had been handed a blueprint for reform with the Murphy inquiry. “This bill is all we get, and frankly, it’s piss weak – it’s a piss weak response to a public health crisis.” Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. title: Say goodbye to bubble wrap: The new products popping the plastic bubble
text:
Advertisement

EnvironmentSustainabilityRecycling Say goodbye to bubble wrap: The new products popping the plastic bubble Caitlin Fitzsimmons August 3, 2026 — 11:59am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

If you walk into a hardware store, you can now find rolls of “bubble wrap” made from paper. The product has the same performance as plastic for about the same price, but the rolls are a lot thinner because it has a honeycomb design rather than air bubbles. Yet the real beauty of it, says Visy chief executive Mark De Wit, is what happens when you are finished with it. Visy chief executive Mark De Wit with a roll of the paper-based alternative to bubble wrap. Dominic Lorrimer “We’ve all had bubble wrap before … it’s a soft plastic so it ends up in landfill, and somewhere between 500 and 1000 years later, it might disintegrate into microplastics,” De Wit said. “This [paper bubble wrap] can go in your recycle bin, and we’ll turn it back into a box within a few weeks of it being collected from your house.” This is just one of a host of innovations in consumer products and packaging that has occurred in the past five years, since this masthead and Visy started hosting an annual recycling roundtable with business leaders and the federal environment minister of the day.

Advertisement

Other examples from Visy alone include cardboard replacements for the plastic protective sheets used by painters and renovators, fruit and vegetable punnets made from recycled cardboard, new insulated material made from reused cardboard to replace polystyrene. Asahi Beverages has replaced the plastic shrink wrap around Carlton Dry six-pack bottles with innovative fibre-board packaging. The company’s Australian primary packaging (excluding caps and labels) was 100 per cent recyclable, reusable or compostable for the first time last year. Nu-Pure has decreased the volume of plastic resin in its water bottles. The company’s 600ml round PET bottle produced in NSW now weighs just 8.59 grams, plus 1.3g for the lid, making it one of the lightest still water bottles in Australia. Several companies are now supplying disposable coffee cups to cafes where the cup and lid are made entirely out of compostable and biodegradeable fibre to Australian standards. Another achievement is that Australian-produced glass now contains 54 per cent recycled content. For Visy, it had increased from 30 per cent to 64 per cent and was expected to reach 70 per cent by next year once the company’s new facility in Yatala, Queensland was complete. This put Australia on par with Germany and New Zealand “and a country mile ahead of everyone else”.

Advertisement

But the failure of the federal and state governments to agree on national packaging standards has stymied growth. Last week, Suzanne Toumbourou, chief executive of the Australian Council of Recycling, put out a statement decrying the lack of federal government action. “Australians are doing their part,” Tomoubourou said. “Recyclers have invested. But the Australian government is betraying that effort by delaying the packaging rules it promised, while more plastic goes to waste and Australian recycling capacity shrinks.” Asahi Beverages chief executive Amanda Sellers and Environment Minister Murray Watt at the 2026 recycling roundtable. Dominic Lorrimer Australians use more than 1.3 million tonnes of plastic packaging every year, but only 19 per cent is collected for recycling, leaving more than one million tonnes to wind up as landfill or litter. Yet Toumbourou said about 320,000 tonnes of Australian plastic reprocessing capacity was standing ready, much of it sitting idle, awaiting the government reforms. This left recyclers in severe commercial peril with some plants facing closure, she said. The industry has been saying for several years that mandatory national standards for packaging are needed so that companies can invest with confidence. The Albanese government has talking about legislation since 2022, but former environment minister Tanya Plibersek and current Environment Minister Murray Watt say the problem has been getting the states and territories to agree.

Advertisement

“When I discuss these things with states, some are completely on board,” Watt said at the roundtable on Friday. “Some are very concerned about what might be quite minimal cost increases for consumers.” Related Article Perspective

Plastic Tooth powder and blocked drains: My week without single-use plastic Watt said packaging would be on the agenda at the next meeting of the federal, state, and territory environment ministers in September. One option for Watt could be using national policy payments to states to encourage them to come on board with national standards. De Wit said the economics of glass, cardboard and aluminium recycling made sense because they were a comparable cost to virgin material. That was not true for hard plastics – including the PET bottles such as water and soft drinks and the HDP bottles such as cloudy milk bottles – because the recycled resin had fixed costs based on collection and processing, while the virgin product was tied to the price of oil and fluctuated wildly. “As a producer of this recycled resin, we see the sales go strong when the virgin price is up here, and then drop off when they’re down here because a lot of companies buy the cheapest, whatever that is, virgin or recycled,” De Wit said.

Advertisement

“What I would like to see is what they’ve done in the 27 EU countries, in the UK, in California, Washington State, New Jersey, where they’ve said because of this exact issue, there has to be 25 per cent minimum recycled content in every plastic bottle.” De Wit said the additional cost would between half and one cent per bottle, so it would “not contribute one iota to a cost of living crisis”. Visy chief Mark De Wit showing an imported drink bottle with a PVC wrapper that contaminates plastic recycling. Dominic Lorrimer Another issue requiring government action was that imported drinks were not held to Australian standards. A plastic drink bottle produced in Australia had to have a wrapper that could be recycled with the bottle. But imported drinks such as those found in Asian supermarkets had PVC wrappers that contaminated the waste stream – one 3g wrapper would contaminate 150 kilograms of PET plastic recycling, which meant 7500 bottles could no longer be processed into food-grade packaging. Arnott’s chief executive George Zoghbi at the recycling roundtable hosted by Visy and this masthead. Dominic Lorrimer

Advertisement

George Zoghbi, chief executive of Arnott’s Biscuits, said he had two things on his wish list. “One is curbside collection for everything, including soft plastic because if you can do that at scale, it changes the game for everybody, and it makes the cost of recycling significantly cheaper, and the take-up rate significantly higher,” Zoghbi said. “The second one is that it’s very hard for consumers to look at these chemical symbols and say which colour bin you should use. Instead, you could put dots on the packaging that matches the colour of the bin – if it’s a red dot, it goes in the red bin; if it’s yellow, it goes in a yellow bin.” This would require states and territories to harmonise their bin collection systems. title: Fool’s gold: Trump is set to break his promise to America
text:
Advertisement

BusinessThe economyTrump's America Opinion Fool’s gold: Trump is set to break his promise to America Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist August 3, 2026 — 11:58am

August 3, 2026 — 11:58am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Who would have thought it? The eurozone, derided by Donald Trump as a declining economy that was heading in the wrong direction, outpaced the US economy in the June quarter. The eurozone economy grew at an annualised rate of 1.8 per cent that quarter, while the US economy grew at 1.5 per cent. Canada, hit hard by Trump’s tariffs, grew its economy over the quarter at an annualised rate of 3.4 per cent. US President Donald Trump, along with his Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, have repeatedly promised a “Golden Age” would arrive this year for the US economy. AP Europe’s growth rate was its fastest in more than a year, despite continuing energy shocks emanating from Trump’s war in the Middle East and his tariffs. In the United States, growth slowed from 2.1 per cent rate in the first three months of the year, despite the continuing boom in artificial intelligence-related investment, lower oil and petrol prices during the ceasefire in the war on Iran and a surge in spending by wealthier Americans (with some assistance from the World Cup) in June.

Advertisement

So much for an economic “Golden Age” for the US that Trump, his Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick have repeatedly promised would arrive this year. So far, the only gold is to be found in the White House, or on Washington’s monuments, where Trump has been gilding anything and everything he can, or in the wealth being accumulated by the Trump family and their associates. Related Article Trump's White House ‘I don’t have inside information’: How Donald Trump Jr is cashing in on dad’s presidency The US economy would probably be running a lot hotter if not for the war in the Middle East and the global war on trade that Trump keeps trying to establish a legal basis for. Along with the data on GDP that was published late last week, the Commerce Department put out personal consumption expenditures (PCE) data for June that showed the US Federal Reserve Board’s preferred measure of inflation, the PCE index, fell 0.1 per cent in June to be 3.7 per cent higher than it was in the same month last year.

Advertisement

While that’s well below the 4.1 per cent May-on-May rate, it is still way above the Fed’s inflation target of 2 per cent. Even stripped of energy and food prices, “core” PCE inflation was 3.3 per cent. In July, hostilities in the Middle East resumed, and oil prices, which had fallen back below $US72 ($102) a barrel in June, spiked again after the brief ceasefire. They surpassed $US100 a barrel last month, before again falling, to about $US84 a barrel at present, as talks appear to have resumed. The US economy would probably be running a lot hotter, if not for the war in the Middle East and the global war on trade that Trump keeps trying to find a legal basis for. Bloomberg US petrol and diesel prices remain well above their prewar levels – petrol about $US1 a gallon higher and diesel about $US1.60 a gallon higher – and will continue to feed into the inflation rate. It is inflation, a declining savings rate, and the fact that much of the equipment required for the boom in AI is imported (and therefore subtracts from GDP) that are weighing on US growth.

Advertisement

For various reasons – not least the stop-start ways in which the trade war, and the real war, have been waged – their impact on the inflation rate and economic growth hasn’t been as significant as most outside the administration had expected. With another newly imposed round of global tariffs on 99.4 per cent of America’s imports, and the war in the Middle East dragging on without any obvious clean conclusion, their effects on the economy and the inflation rate might have been stretched out and delayed, rather than avoided. Related Article Opinion

Interest rates As the Fed sits tight on interest rates, investors take action Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Rather than a one-off shock before prices stabilised, they might still be bleeding into prices and the economy in a fashion that means they may not be “transitory” and therefore can’t be dismissed as such by the Fed, which left its policy rate unchanged – for the fifth successive time – after last week’s meeting. With the Fed’s new Trump-appointed chairman, Kevin Warsh, creating an information vacuum by withdrawing any guidance on interest rates, the bond market has taken matters into its own hands.

Advertisement

The 10-year bond yield is now 4.74 per cent, compared with its pre-meeting level of 4.61 per cent. The 30-year yield has jumped 18 basis points to a 19-year high of 5.27 per cent. Those yields, if sustained, will choke spending and investment and raise the borrowing and refinancing costs on the US government’s debt, which is rapidly nearing $US40 trillion ($57 trillion). So far, the only gold is to be found in the White House, or on Washington’s monuments, where Trump has been gilding anything and everything he can, or in the wealth being accumulated by the Trump family and their associates. Eurozone data shows that its economies – despite being battered by energy-related shocks that began with the war in Ukraine and are continuing with the war in the Middle East, and having to deal with a tide of cheap Chinese imports that has swelled since Trump started building his tariff wall around the US market – are more resilient than expected. All the major economies – Germany, France, Italy and Spain – grew solidly, if not spectacularly, in the quarter, and Ireland, a beneficiary of the AI boom, bounced back from a sharp contraction in the first quarter to growth of 3.9 per cent in the second.

Advertisement

Like most of the rest of the world (China and Canada being the exceptions), while it did threaten action, the eurozone didn’t respond to the US tariffs with retaliatory tariffs – taxes on its consumers – of its own. It’s the US, thanks to the tariffs and the impact of the war-driven higher oil prices on domestic petrol and diesel prices, that is hitting its own businesses and consumers and its own growth hardest. A 1.5 per cent growth rate isn’t a disaster, but it’s hardly the “Golden Age”. The 5 or 6 per cent growth rates that Trump said his policies could generate haven’t materialised (which is no surprise), and neither have the trillions of dollars of foreign investment in the US manufacturing sector that he also said would flow. The Trump family and their associates are accumulating vast amounts of wealth during Donald’s second term. AP Real wages for US workers are declining, manufacturing sector jobs have shrunk, and it is the AI boom and those wealthiest households who benefited most from the tax cuts in Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act and who have gained most from the AI-driven sharemarket wealth effects that are generating the reasonably solid but unspectacular economic growth rate.

Advertisement

If something were to disrupt the AI boom – and investors are getting nervous about the sustainability of the vast amounts of capital being poured into it, by increasingly negative cashflow-generating companies, relative to the cheaper Chinese alternatives and the returns in prospect – the implications for the sharemarket and economy would be threatening. Related Article Opinion

Trump's White House The lyin’ king Trump is the kind of leader the nation’s father feared and reviled Maureen Dowd New York Times columnist Trump and those in his team regularly denigrate the Europeans and their economies, saying the economies are over-regulated, stagnating or declining, being swamped by illegal migrants and effectively subsidised by the US (or leeching off it via unfair terms of trade). Some of those criticisms might be valid, but the Trump alternative of aggressive deregulation, trade barriers and extortion, draconian crackdowns on undocumented migrants and immigration more broadly and a war in the Middle East that is delivering nothing but humiliation and higher energy costs make it difficult for the administration to claim the US, or at least this particular administration, has the superior economic or governance model. title: How the Trump factor finally turned the soccer world against Infantino
text:
Advertisement

SportSoccerFIFA World Cup Opinion How the Trump factor finally turned the soccer world against Infantino

Oliver Brown August 3, 2026 — 11:57am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

It has been soccer’s epiphany – its moment to recognise that its soul is worth saving. A hellish week for Gianni Infantino, whose grand scheme to carve up the World Cup promised to benefit only the private equity boys and his own bank balance, has been a happy one for anybody calling out his cupidity. Gianni Infantino and Donald Trump at the World Cup final. Getty Images This time, the grenades were thrown inside his own building. No sooner did Carlos Cordeiro, his long-time adviser, lambast his shabby back-room plot with Donald Trump’s associates as a “bad deal” than Kevin Lamour, FIFA’s chief operating officer, claimed staff had been “deceived”. The global game has unearthed, albeit belatedly, a few big shots with a spine.

Advertisement

The change in tone is staggering. Once, an organisation such as UEFA would issue only cold, bureaucratic statements. But its latest bulletin, accusing Infantino of seeking to sell off the “family silver” and excoriating the “faceless individuals” who do his bidding, comes dripping in sulphuric acid. It reflects not just the deep disdain of UEFA president Aleksander Čeferin for how his opposite number in Zurich operates, but the righteous indignation that Infantino’s arrogance has unleashed. The World Cup delivered $25 billion in revenue, but that might not save FIFA boss Gianni Infantino. Getty Images While it is rare for soccer to speak as one on any subject, the sheer conceit of a preening Swiss bureaucrat devoid of charm or wit or empathy has united 143 nations and counting in disgust. “In many ways this has been a boost for the principles of football,” says Laura McAllister, Čeferin’s deputy at UEFA. “It’s a validation – football comes out of this stronger.”

Advertisement

It feels necessary, when we so often lament the tin ear of the game’s executives, to give credit where it is due. As soon as UEFA learnt of FIFA’s proposal to hive off the World Cup’s commercial interests for the enrichment of Infantino and Joshua Kushner, the brother of Trump’s son-in-law, it pronounced that it took the move “extremely seriously”. England’s Football Association, likewise, displayed a concern for the common good, declaring that the World Cup “belongs to football and always will”, even if there was the awkward juxtaposition of Debbie Hewitt, the FA chair, turning on Infantino just six weeks after presenting him with a personalised England shirt. In reality, Infantino just looks like a money-grabbing gargoyle in a pair of Stan Smiths. Still, you cannot help but wonder where the red lines are drawn. For a decade, confederations watched the insidious expansion of Infantino’s powers and did nothing. They saw his unctuousness around despotic leaders, his description of feeling like a “child in a toy shop” on visiting Vladimir Putin at the Kremlin, and deemed it a price worth paying. They were so at ease with the World Cup’s enlargement to 48 countries that Infantino felt emboldened, and within days of this summer’s tournament concluding, he set a two-week deadline to approve a 64-team leviathan in 2030.

Advertisement

And the heads of more than 200 national associations clapped like seals when the FIFA president orchestrated the charade of Saudi Arabia’s unopposed bid for the 2034 World Cup, demanding it be rubber-stamped with a round of applause. So why the handbrake turn now? Why, after signing off on so many of his shams, does football regard this example of Infantino’s overreach as beyond the pale? One crucial reason is the Trump factor. Of all the rulers at whose feet Infantino has prostrated himself, the US president has brought out the worst in his grasping, simpering nature. Infantino remains at the centre of a political storm. AP If you found him awarding his friend the inaugural FIFA “Peace Prize” difficult to stomach, you should have tried sitting through his performance at the final World Cup press conference, where he coated Trump in verbal treacle for staging the “greatest human, social and cultural event that mankind has ever witnessed”. He imagines he comes across as the ultimate statesman in such speeches, when in reality he just looks like a money-grabbing gargoyle in a pair of Stan Smiths.

Advertisement

The more the bromance has grown, the more Trumpian Infantino’s behaviour has become. Just as the president arrived late to a G7 summit in Evian this year, crassly joking “I’m the boss”, Infantino pulled the same stunt at FIFA’s 2025 congress in Paraguay, raising UEFA’s hackles by keeping everyone waiting because he had been conducting all-important business in the Gulf with, yes, you guessed it, Trump. Related Article FIFA World Cup Resign or we’ll vote to oust you: Europe’s threat to Infantino Copying his friend’s tiresome “fake news” taunts, he also characterised justified scrutiny of the World Cup as “false rumours” and “hate”. The company of an autocrat seemed to convince him that he, too, was untouchable, or at least that he could shield himself through a cult of personality. Except he never had much of a personality in the first place. You have to marvel at how quickly he has mangled his position of dominance. One minute, he is sitting pretty atop World Cup revenues of more than £13 billion ($25 billion), ready to be re-elected without any rival candidate until 2031. The next he finds himself in apparently terminal peril, an object of universal mockery, with his cynical vision of “FIFA Forward Enterprise” a smouldering shell.

Advertisement

And yet, soccer deludes itself if it imagines its work is complete. Infantino has been so seduced by the trappings of high office that he will fight to retain that cachet like a cornered animal. Even when disavowed by UEFA, CONCACAF and his contacts at Kushner’s Thrive Eternal, he was still scrabbling around to revive the plan with other backers, shameless to the end. The map to his dethroning remains complex. But we should be heartened by the fact that the soccer world, stirred into action by one scandal too many, has rediscovered some semblance of a moral compass. A key member of the right-wing religious group the Reformers moaned that Robert Assaf was paid a $135,000 salary at Catholic Schools NSW to do factional Liberal Party work, text messages shown to a corruption hearing have revealed. Robert Assaf continued giving evidence to the Independent Commission Against Corruption on Monday, where he was asked about a message exchange between fellow Reformers Jean-Claude Perrottet and Christian Ellis. James Brickwood Counsel assisting Dr Peggy Dwyer, SC, read out a text to Ellis, where Perrottet bemoaned that he was doing political work for the right-wing faction without being compensated while claiming Assaf received “$135k for Rob to work for faction”. The commission heard $135,000 was Assaf’s salary at Catholic Schools NSW.

“Can I suggest to you that you were employed in part on the understanding that your work for Reformers would be supported through a salary from Catholic Schools,” Dwyer asked Assaf. “I don’t accept that,” Assaf said. Loading Dwyer also read out some text messages to the commission that show the relationship between Assaf and Ellis becoming frosty over money issues. Assaf said he was entitled to 10 per cent of the total value of contracts with clients he introduced to Ellis’s company Beckington. That included Catholic Schools NSW.

In a text message to Ellis, Assaf said he was “actually quite pissed off” about not getting his cut of the money. Related Article Live

The pair exchanged a few more tense messages before Ellis says: “I think you need to calm down and discussion later. We’ve literally sent some WhatsApp messages back and forth this morning, and you’ve blown up.” Dwyer resumed her questioning of Assaf on Monday asking why he decided to resign from the Reformers, the religious right-wing Liberal factional group that he co-founded.

Assaf told the commission part of his motivation to “phase out” from the Reformers was that he felt the group’s co-founder Ellis was not giving him a straight answer on some of his concerns. One of those concerns, Assaf said, was Ellis’s connection to fugitive Sydney property developer Jean Nassif. Ellis told him he was assisting Nassif with lobbying around a water issue he had for one of his development projects. Assaf said there were widespread concerns, as well as “jokes and insinuations”, in the right faction around Ellis’s connection to Nassif’s Toplace.

“I personally viewed it as a perception issue, like as in you just don’t want to be associated with developers because it really taints the value stuff we were doing,” Assaf said. Assaf also told the commission he became worried the Reformers were spending too much time pursuing a vendetta between the Perrottets and Alex Hawke, of the centre-right faction. Jean-Claude Perrottet was doing a lot of work as part of the Reformers to stack branches in the Hills, where the dispute between Liberal factions was particularly tense. Dwyer asked Assaf about the “vendetta” between the Perrottet brothers and the Hawke faction. Assaf said negative stories about Hawke were part of the “standard brainwashing” members of the right-wing faction got when they joined to explain the factional feud. “The narrative of the right was Hawke equals bad. He backstabbed Dom (Perrottet) at his wedding or something … took branches, split the right, and now Hawke is this kingmaker,” Assaf said.

title: Sydney fuel prices spike as excise discount ends
text:
Advertisement

NationalNSWPetrol prices Sydney fuel prices spike as excise discount ends Daniel Lo Surdo August 3, 2026 — 11:56am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Fuel prices have tipped over $2 a litre in NSW hours after the Albanese government’s fuel excise discount came to an end, triggering fresh warnings of more increases as the prolonged conflict in the Middle East threatens global oil supply. The average price for regular unleaded passed the $2 mark on Monday morning after the fuel excise discount – delivering an approximate 17¢ saving – was withdrawn at midnight. The average national price for unleaded also rose above $2, the first time since May, according to Fuel Check. Petrol prices are expected to steadily rise as the fuel excise returns. Louie Douvis Prices on Monday morning were 13¢ higher than what was recorded in Sydney last week. Sydney petrol prices rose by an average of 2.9¢ a litre overnight, according to the NRMA, less than the 3.2¢ recorded nationally. The highest price for regular in Sydney was at $2.19 in Berowra, and the cheapest $1.84 in Tempe. Tourists enjoying the snow at Thredbo were slugged $2.87 a litre for unleaded on Monday, the most expensive rate in NSW.

Advertisement

NRMA spokesperson Peter Khoury expects retail prices to continue rising this week as the excise is reapplied, but flagged any further rises would depend on developments outside Australia. “The flipside is what actually happens globally to oil prices, we know 17¢ a litre will come in, but if oil prices fall that will negate some of it,” Khoury said. “If we get good news from the Middle East the price will go down, if it doesn’t, it will go back up again.” Jim Chalmers warned service stations they would be watched “like a hawk” for any price gouging. AAPIMAGE Treasurer Jim Chalmers reiterated there were no plans to reintroduce the excise discount – which began in April and was extended ahead of its original end date in July – and warned service stations they would be watched “like a hawk” for any price gouging. “The [Australian Competition and Consumer Commission] has the powers that they need to fine … servos and suppliers up to $100 million per offence, and so servos and suppliers are on notice,” Chalmers told ABC Radio National on Monday morning.

Advertisement

“They can’t use the return to normal settings with the excise as cover for treating motorists as mugs.” Fuel shocks triggered by the Middle East war has led to a surge in the uptake of electric and hybrid vehicles, according to data released by the Australian Automobile Association (AAA) on Sunday. The AAA found almost half of all new car sales in the June quarter were for electric or hybrid vehicles, in what marked the Australia’s largest-ever quarterly rise in EV sales. title: Sydney home sells at a $345,000 loss as auction market tanks
text:
Advertisement

PropertyNewsAuctions Sydney home sells at a $345,000 loss as auction market tanks Carmen Forward August 3, 2026 — 11:47am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A grand family residence in Eastwood that fetched $4.7 million in October last year sold at auction on Saturday for a $345,000 loss as Sydney’s clearance rate fell. The six-bedroom property with gated entrance, brick fireplace and triple lockup garage at 27 Epping Avenue traded for $4,355,000 at the weekend. The property was one of 510 scheduled auctions in Sydney last week. By Saturday evening, Domain Group had recorded a preliminary auction clearance rate of 48 per cent from 289 reported results, while 105 auctions were withdrawn. Withdrawn auctions are counted as unsold properties when calculating the clearance rate. Sydney’s preliminary result is a fall of 5 percentage points from the previous week, and it is likely to be revised lower as more results are collected.

Advertisement

Three buyers registered and two placed bids for the stately Eastwood home with a $4.25 million guide, itself below last year’s sale price. Related Article Auctions ‘More breathing room’: First home buyers pay $1.42m for inner west townhouse Bidding opened at $3.8 million and rose in $100,000 increments until $4.3 million, then the highest bidder bid against himself and added an extra $55,000 to his final offer. The vendors adjusted their $4.5 million reserve to sell, and the hammer fell at $4,355,000. There is no legal requirement for a vendor’s reserve to be in line with their property’s price guide.

Advertisement

Selling agent Andy Lin of Uniland Real Estate, Epping & Castle Hill, said: “The market is still tough. So they are accepting the market.” His vendors are not optimistic about what is happening in the coming year, Lin said. “Happy result for vendors, but the market is still coming down because the interest rate is too high.” Another of his property’s up for auction, at 4 Second Avenue in Epping, passed in. “A lot of auctions [have] got zero buyers at the moment, so auctions that vendors still make a loss … but if they think that they can minimise the loss, they’re still happy,” Lin said.

Advertisement

In Merrylands West, a luxurious property with five bedrooms and six-metre-high ceilings drew zero registrations at auction. The ultra-modern home had curved walls and was on a corner block at 7 Daryl Street. Selling agent Christopher Carey of Citywide Property Agents said four groups had inspected the house, guided with a range of $2.8 million to $2.85 million. Two parties did not register at auction but showed interest. “I think it’s just a wait-and-see kind of thing,” Carey said. “I think a lot of people are doing that at the moment. It’s more of a wait-and-see game. I think they will probably prefer to make a private bid.”

Advertisement

Auctioneer Tom Panos said: “I do 10 to 15 auctions every Saturday … people are withdrawing and cancelling all their auctions. And this one did go ahead, but as there was no one registered, this auction was cancelled as well.” Related Article Auctions ‘Never going to be free’: Sydney clearance rate plummets, more price falls to come “It is very, very clear we are now in a marketplace that has total loss of confidence,” he said. “Buyers are concerned that even though property prices have dropped, that they’re worried that they’re going to further drop, so they’re not buying. “Vendors don’t want to come to the marketplace because they’re seeing what’s happening with the results. “Unfortunately, we’re in a gridlock market, and I don’t think that this was the consequence that the government wanted when they set the budget.”

Advertisement

In Sydney’s east, a two-bedroom single-level garden apartment at Bondi Beach with no parking sold for $2.3 million. The unit at 2/55 Sir Thomas Mitchell Road had a guide of $2 million. Six parties registered to bid, and three of them took part. All were local owner-occupiers. None were investors or first home buyers. Bidding opened at $2 million, jumped to $2.1 million and then rose in $10,000 and $25,000 increments to hit the $2.2 million reserve, before eventually selling for $2.3 million.

Advertisement

Ray White’s Angus Gorrie said buyers were drawn to the “Bondi address”. Related Article NSW residential property The Sydney suburbs where property prices rose – and fell – most “It had a nice courtyard as well, so just giving you that outdoor space. Only four in the block … which people always like.” The vendor is upsizing in the area while the buyer was renting nearby. The address last traded for $1.56 million in 2019, records show. AMP chief economist Dr Shane Oliver said Domain’s clearance rate of 48 per cent for Sydney has “weakened again”.

Advertisement

“The combination of the interest rate hikes, the risk that we might still see more hikes ahead, the tax changes which have sent many investors to the sidelines, along with poor levels of confidence, not helped by the ongoing war with Iran and the rebound in fuel prices. All of those things are keeping buyers very cautious,” he said. Oliver suspects that the clearance rate will remain weak until the year’s end. “At the moment, you’ve got sort of a mismatch between what buyers are prepared to pay and what vendors want,” he said. “Vendors’ expectations are inflated and based on the property on the boom-time conditions that prevailed last year. Those boom-time conditions are long gone.”
