title: Revealed: The extent of tree canopy in your suburb
text:
Advertisement

EnvironmentConservationBiodiversity Revealed: The extent of tree canopy in your suburb Caitlin Fitzsimmons August 3, 2026 — 11:45am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

New suburbs in western Sydney not only have the least tree canopy coverage in the city but will also remain hot “moonscapes” because developers did not leave enough space to plant big trees, experts say. Greater Sydney will struggle to almost double tree canopy across the city to 40 per cent by 2036, as well, because the current growth rate is just a tenth of a percentage point a year. Greater Sydney is in need of root and branch reform: North Sydney’s winter canopy this month. Steven Siewert Figures published by the Department of Planning, Housing and Infrastructure suggest that Greater Sydney’s tree canopy lifted slightly from 21.7 per cent in 2022-23 to 21.9 per cent in 2024-25. At that rate, it would reach 23 per cent by 2036. A department spokesperson said the government was spending more than $60 million through the Greening our City program to help councils in Greater Sydney, the Illawarra-Shoalhaven and the Hunter-Central Coast plant trees and biodiverse understorey in parks, streets and neighbourhoods. More than half a million trees had been planted through large-scale partnerships between 2020 and the end of 2025, the spokesperson said.

Advertisement

“Research shows trees can reduce ground-level temperatures by up to six degrees, while communities with more than 30 per cent canopy cover experience improved mental and physical health outcomes,” the spokesperson said. Gwilym Griffiths, co-founder of the Good Canopy Company, which helps local governments with urban forest management and planning, said the 40 per cent target was “aspirational and admirable … but in terms of being realistic, no, I don’t think it is, and this latest data set just really proves that”.

Advertisement

The more important part of the puzzle, Griffiths said, was the location of trees and the fact that the communities facing the greatest heat exposure were often the ones with the least canopy. Some of the suburbs with the least canopy are new master-planned subdivisions in western Sydney, such as Melonba in Blacktown Council area with 4.01 per cent canopy, and Oran Park and Gregory Hills in Camden Council area with 4.12 per cent and 4.42 per cent, respectively. “Housing and canopy ... need to be delivered as one, and we shouldn’t have to choose,” Griffiths said. “Good density can retain trees, and it can leave space for trees and treat trees as essential infrastructure.” Peter Davies, professor of sustainability at Macquarie University, agreed that the 40 per cent target was unrealistic. “I understand the pressure to deliver housing, but there’s no point having lots of housing if it’s hot, there’s no aesthetic and it’s just not comfortable,” he said.

Advertisement

Western Sydney University Professor Sebastian Pfautsch walks down the middle of the trees on the median strip on Norwest Boulevard in Norwest, an example of good urban design that can help to combat climate change and heat stress in western Sydney. Janie Barrett A development in Marsden Park with small to medium street trees. Janie Barrett Sebastian Pfautsch, a professor of urban management and planning at Western Sydney University, said most of these new developments were built on former paddocks, so there were not many existing trees. “After some kind of arborist assessment, you have a group of trees that you identify that then become park trees in your new public park, and that’s it, there’s nothing else,” Pfautsch said. “It’s what we call moonscaping.” The subdivisions are then left without any space or deep soil for trees in backyards, while the streets are planted with small trees such as water gums and crepe myrtles, or medium species such as paperbarks and bottle brushes that do not provide much shade.

Advertisement

Pfautsch said a PhD student at WSU had just completed a project that showed that in a place such as Kellyville, current planting of street trees would achieve only 6 to 9 per cent canopy in the next 20 years. Even growing the tallest species on all available public land would reach just 26 per cent canopy as there was no space for trees in private yards. The leafy north shore lives up to its name, with 80.31 per cent tree canopy in Ku-ring-gai Chase, 43.7 per cent in Pymble and 34.96 per cent in Mosman. The analysis counts only the parts of the suburb in the metropolitan urban area, meaning council-controlled bushland is counted but not national parks. In the inner city, Balmain has 22.89 per cent tree canopy, Darlinghurst has 22.77 per cent and Newtown 22.47 per cent. “At least when you mention Darlinghurst or Newtown, you will still find some gardens in places, so you will still find some private canopy,” Pfautsch said. “You don’t have anything like that in the new suburbs in western Sydney.” Davies said that most councils had good guidelines for canopy and landscaping in development control plans, and the NSW Government Architect also had good advice, but none of it was mandatory.

Advertisement

Tree canopy was under pressure in established leafy areas as well, Davies said. “Even though you’ve got to go to council to get permission to cut down a tree, it’s a difficult one for councils because often their decisions are lot by lot, and they don’t account for the cumulative impact,” Davies said. The tree canopy was measured with aerial photography, and the department used the same methodology and suburb and LGA boundaries for the comparison between 2022-23 and 2024-25. title: New Premier’s surprise cabinet decision
text:
The new Victorian Premier will look to save hundreds of thousands of dollars by cutting the number of ministers in cabinet.

With specific portfolios set to be announced on Tuesday, new Premier Ben Carroll announced Monday only one of three cabinet vacancies will be filled ahead of the November election.

"It doesn't pass the pub test having multiple ministers signed in 12 weeks out before a campaign begins," he said.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

"So we're reducing the size of the ministry as a simple measure, but a demonstration of my commitment to taxpayers' dollars."

Newly appointed minister Tim Richardson and Deputy Premier Gabrielle Williams flanked Premier Ben Carroll for the announcement on Monday. Picture: NewsWire / Andrew Henshaw

Non-minister MPs receive a salary a tick over $219,000, while ministers get an extra $184,407 plus nearly $20,000 in allowances.

The new 20-person cabinet consists of 11 women and nine men.

With deposed former premier Jacinta Allan out of cabinet, along with her allies Harriet Shing and Lily D'Ambrosio, Mr Carroll announced on Monday that Tim Richardson had been elevated to cabinet.

Mr Carroll declined to put an exact dollar figure on the savings, nor confirm if the smaller cabinet would be a feature of a re-elected Labor government.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

"Every dollar should be spent wisely, considerately, and where it delivers the best value for money," he said.

"This is a considerable saving.

"We'll have more to say on this in the future."

Ben Carroll was sworn in as Premier last week. Picture: NewsWire / David Caird

Long-time MP Lily D'Ambrosia was one of two Jacinta Allan allies to quit cabinet shortly after. Picture: NewsWire / David Caird

Mr Carroll will announce who gets which portfolios on Tuesday.

Following Ms Allan's resignation last week, Ms Shing and Ms D'Ambrosio resigned from cabinet and announced they would not seek re-election at the November 28 poll.

Both departing senior MPs backed Mr Carroll "against the Liberal Party and One Nation in November".

Ms Allan's Socialist Left faction will still form the majority of the cabinet. New deputy premier Gabrielle Williams is expected to take Mr Carroll's education portfolio, ahead of another statewide public teacher strike in two weeks.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

Newly promoted minister Mr Richardson backed Attorney-General Sonia Kilkenny to take the leadership during a chaotic week last week.

Asked on Monday if Mr Carroll could trust Mr Richardson, Mr Richardson said the cabinet "know my values".

"They know that over the next 117 days I will leave absolutely everything on the field; 100 per cent in my support of the Premier and deputy premier," he said.

title: ‘Shop smarter’: Aussies hit by fuel spike
text:
Drivers are being urged to "shop smarter" for fuel as prices spike from the end of the federal government's fuel excise cut.

The NRMA said national unleaded petrol prices had risen on average by 3.2 cents per litre on Monday after the removal of the fuel excise discount.

It said the gaps in price between fuel types had reached a "record high" and urged motorists to consider cheaper alternatives where possible.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

"With the excise going up today and the war continuing, finding smart ways to save at the bowser remain critical for many Australian struggling with cost-of-living pressures," NRMA spokesman Peter Khoury said.

The difference in prices between fuel categories has reached 'record highs'. Picture: NewsWire / Nikki Short

"Not paying premium prices for premium fuels if you don't have to is a great place to start."

Diesel had also increased on average by 3.4 cents per litre," Mr Khoury said.

Adelaide was hit the hardest with an almost 4 cent per litre jump in both categories, while Perth experienced a 5.1 cent per litre increase in diesel.

The price difference between E10 and Premium 98 fuel has also reached a national record high of a 30.5 cents per litre gap.

NRMA spokesman Peter Khoury has urged drivers to 'shop smarter' at the fuel bowser. Picture: NewsWire / Gaye Gerard

A difference of 26.5 cents per litre was also recorded between E10 and 98 in Sydney, marking the most expensive gap since 2012.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

Premium 95 also broke records when compared with E10, rising to a 19.1 cents per litre difference nationally from the previous record of 13 cents per litre.

Mr Khoury said motorists could save up to $17 on a standard 55-litre tank and support locally sourced biofuels by opting for E10.

"It is absolutely critical that Australians understand that they have choice at the bowser," he said.

"Supporting this industry is an effective way to boost jobs regionally and reduce our dependence on imported oil."

The national average in price between E10 and Premium 98 has reached 30.5 cents per litre. Picture: NewsWire / Nikki Short

Jim Chalmers raised concerns about service stations hiking up prices on Friday.

The Treasurer wrote to the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) chair Gina Cass-Gottlieb calling for increased "scrutiny of fuel prices as fuel excise rates return to their normal settings".

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

"The restoration of excise rates to normal settings cannot be used as a pretext for false, misleading or otherwise unjustified price increases," the letter stated.

"I expect the ACCC to investigate any concerns regarding misrepresentations about petrol prices, false and misleading conduct or anti-competitive conduct in petrol markets and to take appropriate action."

Treasurer Jim Chalmers has called on the ACCC to crack down on service stations taking advantage of the transition. Picture: NewsWire/ Tertius Pickard

Mr Chalmers said any price increase that could not be explained "will face serious scrutiny from the ACCC".

"We've jacked up the penalties for petrol stations that rip off Australians. They face multimillion-dollar fines if they break the law," he said.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

Mr Khoury said the NRMA was also "monitoring prices carefully" and current prices indicated petrol stations were following guidelines.

"Those increases give us confidence that petrol stations are doing the right thing," he said.

The heavy vehicle road user charge will also return to its normal rate of 32.4 cents per litre on Monday after it was cut to 16.4 cents per litre for liquid fuels such as diesel.
